Straight water waves of wavelength 2.0 cm pass through a gap in a barrier. For which gap width is the spreading of the waves (diffraction) greatest?
A 2.0 cm
B 6.0 cm
C 10 cm
D 20 cm
parts.answer: A 2.0 cm
parts.working: Diffraction is greatest when the gap is about the same size as the wavelength; the 2.0 cm gap equals the wavelength, so the waves spread out most (almost semicircular wavefronts). With the 20 cm gap the waves pass through almost straight, with spreading only at the edges.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a water wave, the horizontal distance from a crest to the next trough is 12 cm. What is the wavelength?
A 6 cm
B 12 cm
C 24 cm
D 48 cm
parts.answer: C 24 cm
parts.working: A crest to the next trough is half a wavelength, so λ = 2 × 12 = 24 cm. 12 cm is the common error of treating crest-to-trough as a full wavelength.

practice.stem: A long rope is shaken from one end. At one instant, crests are seen at distances of 0, 0.80 m, 1.60 m and 2.40 m from the hand. Each crest is 5.0 cm above the rest position of the rope. A student counts 12 crests passing a mark in 4.0 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the wavelength and the amplitude of the wave.
parts.answer: wavelength 0.80 m; amplitude 5.0 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the wave.
parts.answer: 3.0 Hz

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the wave along the rope.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the period of the wave.

practice.stem: Water waves in a ripple tank travel at 24 cm/s in deep water and have a wavelength of 3.0 cm. They pass into shallow water where their wavelength becomes 2.0 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the waves.
parts.answer: 8.0 Hz

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the waves in the shallow water.
parts.answer: 16 cm/s

parts.label: c
parts.text: The boundary is at an angle to the wavefronts. Describe what happens to the direction of the waves and name the effect.
parts.answer: The waves change direction, bending towards the normal to the boundary; this is refraction.
parts.working: B1 change of direction (towards normal in slower medium); B1 refraction

practice.stem: In a valley in Gilgit-Baltistan surrounded by high ridges, a family can receive a long-wave radio station of frequency 200 kHz, but mobile-phone signals of frequency 900 MHz from a mast beyond the ridge are very weak.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of each signal. The speed of radio waves is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
parts.answer: Long-wave: 1500 m; mobile: 0.33 m
parts.working: C1 λ = v ÷ f; A1 both: 1500 m and 0.33 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why the long-wave signal is still received in the valley but the mobile signal is weak.
parts.answer: Diffraction is significant when the wavelength is comparable with the size of the obstacle/gap; the 1500 m waves diffract (bend) round the mountain ridges into the valley; the 0.33 m waves are far smaller than the hills, diffract very little, so the valley is in a 'shadow'.
parts.working: B1 long wavelength diffracts more; B1 comparable to size of hills/ridges so bends round into the valley; B1 short wavelength hardly diffracts – shadow region.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe, in words, the pattern of wavefronts produced when plane waves pass through a gap much wider than their wavelength. Mention the wavelength.
parts.answer: Mostly straight wavefronts continue through the gap with only slight curving at the edges; the wavelength is unchanged.
parts.working: B1 mainly straight with slight bending at edges; B1 same wavelength (spacing) after the gap.

practice.stem: A tsunami crosses the deep Indian Ocean at a speed of 200 m/s. The time between one wave crest and the next passing a buoy is 600 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the tsunami.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the tsunami in the deep ocean. Give your answer in km.
parts.answer: 120 km
parts.working: C1 λ = v × T (= v ÷ f); A1 120 km.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Near the coast the speed falls to 20 m/s. Calculate the new wavelength.
parts.answer: 12 km

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the frequency of the wave does not change when it moves into shallow water.
parts.answer: The frequency is set by the source; the number of waves arriving per second must equal the number leaving per second.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest why the height of the wave increases as it approaches the coast.
parts.answer: The waves slow down and bunch up (shorter wavelength), so the same energy is concentrated into a shorter length of water, giving a larger amplitude.

practice.stem: A seismic station in Quetta records waves from an earthquake. P-waves travel through the rock at 6.0 km/s and S-waves at 3.5 km/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which type of wave arrives first and explain why.
parts.answer: The P-wave, because it travels faster.

parts.label: b
parts.text: S-waves are transverse and P-waves are longitudinal. State what this means for the motion of the ground as each wave passes.
parts.answer: P-wave: ground moves back and forth along the direction of travel. S-wave: ground moves at right angles to the direction of travel.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The S-wave arrives 40 s after the P-wave. Calculate the distance from the station to the earthquake.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sea waves of wavelength 12 m reach a harbour entrance. Compare the diffraction when the entrance is 15 m wide and when it is 120 m wide.
parts.answer: 15 m (similar to the wavelength): strong spreading into the harbour; 120 m (much wider): little spreading, waves continue mostly straight.
parts.working: B1 narrow gap gives much diffraction; B1 wide gap gives little

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a harbour designer would choose a narrow entrance.
parts.answer: Waves spread out after the gap so their energy is spread over a wide area, making the water calmer in the harbour (less wave energy enters).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the wavelengths in air of a 100 Hz sound and a 10 kHz sound. (Speed of sound = 340 m/s)
parts.working: M1 λ = v ÷ f; A1 both

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why the bass notes of music from a wedding party next door are heard around the corner of a building more clearly than the high notes.
parts.answer: Bass wavelengths (metres) are similar to the size of doorways/building edges, so they diffract strongly; high notes have much shorter wavelengths and diffract little.
parts.working: B1 long wavelength comparable to gap/obstacle; B1 more diffraction for bass

parts.label: a
parts.text:
White light passes through a glass prism and forms a spectrum on a screen. Which colour is refracted the most?
A red
B yellow
C green
D violet
parts.answer: D violet
parts.working: Violet light has the highest refractive index in glass (it travels slowest), so it is deviated the most; red is deviated the least.

practice.stem: A boy in Bahawalpur holds a converging lens above a sheet of paper on a sunny day. He moves the lens until a small bright image of the Sun appears. The distance from the lens to the paper is then 12 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the principal focus of a converging lens.
parts.answer: The point on the principal axis through which rays parallel to the axis pass after refraction by the lens.
parts.working: B1 rays parallel to principal axis; B1 converge to / pass through a point on the axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the image of the Sun forms at a distance equal to the focal length.
parts.answer: The Sun is so far away that its rays arriving at the lens are parallel, so they meet at the principal focus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The boy finds that the paper becomes very hot at the bright spot. Explain why.
parts.answer: The lens concentrates the light (and infrared) energy from a large area into a small spot.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one safety precaution he should take.
parts.answer: Never look at the Sun through the lens; do it on a non-flammable surface / keep away from dry grass.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A converging lens is used as a magnifying glass. Which describes the image?
A real, inverted, enlarged
B virtual, upright, enlarged
C virtual, inverted, diminished
D real, upright, same size
parts.answer: B virtual, upright, enlarged
parts.working: With the object closer than the principal focus, the image is virtual, upright and magnified. A describes a projector image (object between F and 2F).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the principal axis of a lens.
parts.answer: The line through the optical centre of the lens at right angles to the lens.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by the focal length of a converging lens.
parts.answer: The distance from the optical centre to the principal focus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between a real image and a virtual image.
parts.answer: A real image is formed where rays actually meet and can be shown on a screen; a virtual image is where rays only appear to come from and cannot be formed on a screen.
parts.working: B1 real: rays meet, on screen; B1 virtual: rays appear to diverge from it, not on screen

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to a beam of parallel light passing through a diverging lens.
parts.answer: The rays spread out (diverge) as if coming from a point on the same side as the incoming light: the principal focus.
parts.working: B1 rays spread out; B1 appear to come from the principal focus

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of image always formed by a diverging lens of a real object.
parts.answer: Virtual, upright and diminished.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which defect of vision is corrected by a diverging lens.
parts.answer: Short sight.

practice.stem: A converging lens has a focal length of 10 cm. An object is placed on the principal axis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the image formed when the object is 25 cm from the lens. State where it forms.
parts.answer: Real, inverted, diminished; on the opposite side of the lens, between 10 cm and 20 cm from it (between F and 2F).
parts.working: B1 real and inverted; B1 diminished (smaller); B1 position between F and 2F on the other side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, in words, the two rays you would draw to locate this image on a ray diagram.
parts.answer: A ray from the top of the object parallel to the principal axis, which refracts through the principal focus on the far side; a ray from the top of the object straight through the optical centre, undeviated.
parts.working: B1 each (accept a ray through the near focus emerging parallel).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The object is moved to 6 cm from the lens. Describe the image now and state one use of the lens in this arrangement.
parts.answer: Virtual, upright, magnified, on the same side as the object; used as a magnifying glass.
parts.working: B1 virtual and upright; B1 magnified; B1 magnifying glass.

practice.stem: Ayesha and her grandfather both visit an optician in Rawalpindi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha is short-sighted. Describe what she sees and state where the image of a distant object forms in her eye.
parts.answer: Distant objects look blurred (near objects are clear); the image forms in front of the retina.
parts.working: B1 distant objects blurred; B1 image in front of retina.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of lens used to correct short sight and explain how it works.
parts.answer: A diverging (concave) lens; it spreads the rays out before they enter the eye so the eye lens focuses them further back, on the retina.
parts.working: B1 diverging lens; B1 rays diverged so image moves back onto retina.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Her grandfather is long-sighted. State the type of lens he needs and where the image would form without it.
parts.answer: Converging (convex) lens; without it the image of a near object forms behind the retina.
parts.working: B1 converging; B1 behind the retina.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a camera, the object is further than 2f from the lens. Describe the image formed on the sensor.
parts.answer: Real, inverted, diminished (between f and 2f behind the lens).

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a slide projector, the slide is placed between f and 2f from the lens. Describe the image and state where it forms.
parts.answer: Real, inverted, magnified; beyond 2f on the other side of the lens (on the screen).
parts.working: B2 three properties (B1 for two); B1 beyond 2f

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the slide must be put into the projector upside down.
parts.answer: The image is inverted, so an upside-down slide gives an upright picture on the screen.

practice.stem: A 2.0 cm tall object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 15 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where the image forms and describe it.
parts.answer: 30 cm from the lens on the other side; real, inverted, same size.
parts.working: B1 30 cm (at 2F); B2 three properties (B1 for two)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the height of the image.
parts.answer: 2.0 cm

parts.label: c
parts.text: The object is moved to 20 cm from the lens and the image is now 6.0 cm tall. Calculate the magnification.
parts.working: M1 magnification = image height ÷ object height = 6.0 ÷ 2.0; A1 3.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the colours of the visible spectrum, in order from the least refracted to the most refracted.
parts.answer: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
parts.working: B2 all in order (B1 if one out of place)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why white light splits into colours in a glass prism.
parts.answer: Each colour travels at a different speed in glass so has a slightly different refractive index; they refract by different amounts (violet most).
parts.working: B1 different speeds / refractive indices; B1 different angles of refraction

parts.label: c
parts.text: A second prism is placed upside down next to the first. State what is seen on the screen.
parts.answer: The colours recombine to give white light.

practice.stem:
On graph paper, a thin converging lens lies along the y-axis with its optical centre at (0, 0); the principal axis is the x-axis and 1 unit = 1 cm. The focal length is 4 cm, so a principal focus is at (4, 0). An object is a vertical arrow from (−12, 0) to (−12, 3).
Ray 1 leaves the top of the arrow parallel to the axis, reaches the lens at (0, 3) and is refracted through (4, 0).
Ray 2 leaves the top of the arrow and passes straight through the optical centre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the equation of the line followed by ray 1 after it passes through the lens.
parts.answer: It passes through (0, 3) and (4, 0): y = 3 − 0.75x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the equation of the line followed by ray 2.
parts.answer: It passes through (−12, 3) and (0, 0): y = −0.25x.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates where the rays meet. Hence state the position and height of the image.
parts.answer: (6, −1.5); the image is 6 cm from the lens on the opposite side and 1.5 cm tall.
parts.working: M1 3 − 0.75x = −0.25x; A1 x = 6, y = −1.5; B1 image 6 cm from lens, height 1.5 cm.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the image fully (three properties).
parts.answer: Real, inverted, diminished (half the size of the object).

practice.stem: A narrow beam of white light enters a glass prism at an angle of incidence of 50°. The refractive index of the glass is 1.51 for red light and 1.53 for violet light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the angle of refraction in the glass for the red light and for the violet light.
parts.answer: Red: 30.5°; violet: 30.0°
parts.working: C1 sin r = sin 50° ÷ n; A1 red 30.5°; A1 violet 30.0°.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angle between the red and violet rays inside the glass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of speed, why the colours separate.
parts.answer: Different colours (frequencies) travel at different speeds in glass, so they have different refractive indices; violet slows most and is refracted most, red least.
parts.working: B1 different speeds / refractive indices for different colours; B1 violet refracted more than red.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what is meant by monochromatic light.
parts.answer: Light of a single frequency (single colour / wavelength).

practice.stem: On graph paper (1 unit = 1 cm) a thin diverging lens lies along the y-axis with its optical centre at (0, 0). The principal axis is the x-axis. The focal length is 10 cm, so the principal focus on the object side is at (-10, 0). An object 3.0 cm tall stands on the axis with its base at (-15, 0), so its top is at (-15, 3).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ray 1 leaves the top of the object parallel to the principal axis, reaches the lens at (0, 3) and then travels as if it came from the principal focus at (-10, 0). Write down the equation of ray 1 after the lens.
parts.working: B1 line through (0, 3) and (-10, 0): slope = 3 ÷ 10 = 0.3, so y = 3 + 0.3x

parts.label: b
parts.text: Ray 2 leaves the top of the object and passes undeviated through the optical centre. Write down the equation of ray 2.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The two rays diverge after the lens. Extend them backwards to find where they appear to meet. State the position and height of the image.
parts.answer: They appear to meet at (-6, 1.2): the image is 6 cm from the lens on the same side as the object and is 1.2 cm tall.
parts.working: M1 solve 3 + 0.3x = -0.2x, so x = -6; A1 y = -0.2 × (-6) = 1.2; A1 image 6 cm from the lens, 1.2 cm tall, same side as the object

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the image fully and give its magnification.
parts.answer: Virtual, upright, diminished; magnification = 0.40 (1.2 ÷ 3.0)
parts.working: B1 three properties: virtual, upright, diminished (B1 for two); B1 magnification = image height ÷ object height = 1.2 ÷ 3.0 = 0.40

practice.stem: An object is moved slowly along the principal axis towards a converging lens of focal length 10 cm, starting 50 cm away and ending 5 cm away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the image changes as the object is moved from 50 cm to just over 20 cm from the lens.
parts.answer: The image stays real and inverted; it moves further from the lens and grows from diminished to the same size at 20 cm (2f).
parts.working: B1 image moves away from lens; B1 grows to same size at 2f

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the image when the object is 15 cm from the lens.
parts.answer: Real, inverted, magnified, formed beyond 2f (more than 20 cm away).
parts.working: B1 real inverted magnified; B1 beyond 2f

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens when the object is exactly 10 cm from the lens.
parts.answer: The rays leave parallel and no image is formed (image at infinity).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the image when the object is 5 cm from the lens.
parts.answer: Virtual, upright, magnified, on the same side as the object.
parts.working: B1 virtual upright; B1 magnified / same side

practice.stem: A glass has a refractive index of 1.50 for red light and 1.54 for violet light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of red light and of violet light in the glass. (Speed of light in air = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
parts.answer: red 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s; violet 1.95 × 10⁸ m/s
parts.working: M1 v = c ÷ n; A1 both

parts.label: b
parts.text: A short pulse of white light travels 10 cm through the glass along the normal. Calculate how much later the violet light emerges than the red light.
parts.working: M1 Δt = 0.10 × (1.54 − 1.50) ÷ 3.0 × 10⁸ (or difference of two times); A1 1.33 × 10⁻¹¹ s

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why white light entering the glass along the normal is not split into colours.
parts.answer: Along the normal there is no change in direction for any colour, so the colours stay together even though they travel at different speeds.
parts.working: B1 angle of incidence 0° so no refraction (bending); B1 all colours follow same path

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the approximate range of frequencies that a healthy human ear can hear?
A 2 Hz to 2000 Hz
B 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
C 200 Hz to 200 000 Hz
D 20 kHz to 200 kHz
parts.answer: B 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz
parts.working: The audible range is about 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Frequencies above 20 kHz (option D) are ultrasound.

practice.stem: An electric bell is hung inside a sealed glass jar. The bell is switched on and air is then slowly pumped out of the jar.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the sound heard as the air is pumped out, and explain why.
parts.answer: The sound becomes quieter and then cannot be heard (though the bell is still seen vibrating), because sound needs a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum.
parts.working: B1 sound fades / disappears; B1 sound needs a medium (cannot travel in vacuum).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how sound travels through air, using the words compression and rarefaction.
parts.answer: The vibrating source pushes air particles back and forth along the direction of travel, producing regions of high pressure (compressions) and low pressure (rarefactions) that travel outwards.
parts.working: B1 particles vibrate parallel to direction of travel (longitudinal); B1 compressions and rarefactions passed on.

parts.label: c
parts.text: List solids, liquids and gases in order of the speed of sound in them, fastest first.
parts.answer: Solids, liquids, gases.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change in a sound wave makes the note sound higher in pitch?
A a larger amplitude
B a higher frequency
C a longer wavelength in the same material
D a lower speed
parts.answer: B a higher frequency
parts.working: Pitch depends on frequency: higher frequency, higher pitch. A larger amplitude (A) makes the sound louder, not higher.

practice.stem: A dhol (a double-sided drum) is played at a wedding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the drum produces a sound.
parts.answer: The drum skin vibrates; it pushes and pulls the air next to it, producing compressions and rarefactions that travel as a sound wave.
parts.working: B1 skin vibrates; B1 makes air particles vibrate / compressions and rarefactions

parts.label: b
parts.text: The drummer hits the drum harder. State the effect on the amplitude and on the loudness.
parts.answer: The amplitude increases, so the sound is louder.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why sound cannot travel through outer space.
parts.answer: There are no particles (it is a vacuum) to pass on the vibrations.

practice.stem: On a sports ground, a teacher fires a starting pistol 500 m from a student. The student starts a stopwatch when she sees the smoke and stops it when she hears the bang. The time is 1.48 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of sound.
parts.answer: 338 m/s (about 340 m/s)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the timer starts the watch when she sees the smoke rather than when she hears the bang.
parts.answer: Light travels so fast that its travel time is negligible, but the sound takes 1.48 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways of making the result more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat several times and take the average; use a larger distance; swap positions to cancel wind effects; use several timers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by ultrasound.
parts.answer: Sound with a frequency above 20 kHz (above the upper limit of human hearing).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two uses of ultrasound.
parts.answer: Scanning a foetus in the womb; cleaning delicate objects/jewellery; checking metal for cracks; echo sounding of the sea bed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why ultrasound, not X-rays, is used to check a baby in the womb.
parts.answer: Ultrasound is not ionising, so it does not harm the developing baby's cells.

practice.stem: Two students stand 85 m from a high wall of their school in Hyderabad. One claps two wooden blocks and the other measures the time until the echo is heard as 0.50 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed of sound given by this measurement.
parts.working: C1 total distance = 2 × 85 = 170 m; A1 v = 170 ÷ 0.50 = 340 m/s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why timing one echo with a hand-held stopwatch is not reliable.
parts.answer: 0.50 s is short compared with human reaction time (about 0.2 s), so the percentage error is large.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the students could improve the method.
parts.answer: Clap repeatedly so each clap coincides with the echo of the previous one; time 20 (or more) claps and divide; repeat and average.
parts.working: B1 time many intervals/claps and divide; B1 repeat and average / use a larger distance.

practice.stem: A fishing ship near Gwadar uses an echo sounder. A pulse of ultrasound is sent straight down and the echo from the sea bed returns 0.8 s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by ultrasound.
parts.answer: Sound with a frequency above 20 kHz (above the human hearing range).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the depth of the sea below the ship.
parts.working: C1 distance = speed × time ÷ 2; A1 600 m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A deeper part of the sea gives an echo that is quieter. State the property of the sound wave that has changed and how it has changed.
parts.answer: The amplitude is smaller.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State how the pitch of a sound is related to its frequency.
parts.answer: Higher frequency gives a higher pitch.

practice.stem: Saima stands between two cliffs in a valley in the Hunza region and shouts. She hears the first echo from the nearer cliff after 1.8 s. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance from Saima to the first cliff.

parts.label: b
parts.text: She hears a second echo, from a cliff on the opposite side, after 2.6 s. Calculate the distance to this cliff.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the width of the valley between the two cliffs.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why the second echo is quieter than the first.
parts.answer: The sound travels further, so it spreads out more and loses more energy (smaller amplitude).

practice.stem: A microphone is connected to an oscilloscope whose time-base is set at 1.0 ms per division. The screen is 10 divisions wide. For sound X there are exactly 4 complete waves across the screen. For sound Y there are exactly 6 complete waves across the screen, with the same height as for X.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period and frequency of sound X.
parts.answer: period 2.5 ms; frequency 400 Hz
parts.working: M1 one wave = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 divisions; A1 T = 2.5 ms; A1 f = 1 ÷ 0.0025 = 400 Hz

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of sound Y.
parts.answer: 600 Hz

parts.label: c
parts.text: Compare the two sounds as heard by the student.
parts.answer: Y has a higher pitch (higher frequency); both are equally loud (same amplitude).

practice.stem: A railway worker strikes a steel rail with a hammer. A second worker, 1020 m away with an ear near the rail, hears two sounds: one through the rail and one through the air. The speed of sound in steel is 5100 m/s and in air is 340 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time for the sound to travel along the rail.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for the sound to travel through the air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the time interval between the two sounds heard by the worker.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why sound travels faster in steel than in air.
parts.answer: Particles in a solid are very close together and strongly bonded, so vibrations are passed on much more quickly.
parts.working: B1 particles close together; B1 strong forces pass vibration quickly

practice.stem: During a storm over Lahore, Bilal sees a flash of lightning and hears the thunder 4.5 s later. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance to the lightning.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the time for the light to reach Bilal is negligible. The speed of light is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
parts.answer: t = 1530 ÷ 3.0 × 10⁸ = 5.1 µs, far less than 4.5 s (and reaction time).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A tuning fork of frequency 256 Hz is struck. Calculate the wavelength of the sound in air and in water. The speed of sound in water is 1480 m/s.
parts.answer: Air: 1.33 m; water: 5.78 m

parts.label: d
parts.text: The tuning fork is struck harder. State and explain how the sound heard changes, and whether its wavelength changes.
parts.answer: It sounds louder because the amplitude is larger; the pitch and wavelength do not change (frequency and speed unchanged).
parts.working: B1 louder – larger amplitude; B1 wavelength unchanged.

practice.stem: An ultrasound probe on a patient's skin sends short pulses into the body. Echoes come back from two boundaries after 65 µs and 91 µs. The speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1540 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the depth of each boundary below the probe.
parts.answer: 5.0 cm and 7.0 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence calculate the thickness of the layer between the two boundaries.
parts.answer: 2.0 cm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a gel is placed between the probe and the skin.
parts.answer: To remove the air gap, so that ultrasound passes into the body instead of being reflected at the skin.

practice.stem: A bat hunting at dusk sends out ultrasound calls of frequency 50 kHz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the bat's call in air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The echo from a moth returns 12 ms after the call. Calculate the distance to the moth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why bats use such high frequencies to find small insects.
parts.answer: High frequency gives a very short wavelength, similar in size to the insect, so the waves reflect from it rather than diffracting around it.
parts.working: B1 short wavelength; B1 comparable to insect size so it is detected / less diffraction around it

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the wavelengths in air at the lower and upper limits of human hearing. (Speed of sound = 340 m/s)
parts.working: M1 λ = v ÷ f with 20 Hz and 20 kHz; A1 both

parts.label: b
parts.text: A dog whistle produces sound of frequency 25 kHz. Explain why the dog hears it but its owner does not.
parts.answer: 25 kHz is above 20 kHz, the upper limit for humans, but within a dog's hearing range.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the dog-whistle sound in air.

parts.label: d
parts.text: As people get older they often cannot hear very high frequencies. Suggest one effect this could have on how well they hear speech in a noisy room.
parts.answer: They miss high-frequency consonant sounds (like 's' and 't'), so speech is less clear.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which list puts parts of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing wavelength?
A gamma rays, ultraviolet, infrared, microwaves
B microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma rays
C ultraviolet, gamma rays, microwaves, infrared
D infrared, microwaves, gamma rays, ultraviolet
parts.answer: A gamma rays, ultraviolet, infrared, microwaves
parts.working: Shortest to longest: gamma, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio. B is the order of increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength).

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of microwaves, ultraviolet and X-rays, state one use.
parts.answer: Microwaves: cooking / mobile phones / satellite communication. Ultraviolet: detecting fake bank notes / sterilising water. X-rays: medical images of bones / airport security scanners.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For ultraviolet and X-rays, state one harmful effect on people.
parts.answer: Ultraviolet: damage to skin cells – sunburn / skin cancer / eye damage. X-rays: mutation or damage to cells, can cause cancer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one property shared by all electromagnetic waves.
parts.answer: They all travel at the same speed (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s) in a vacuum / are transverse / need no medium.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which quantity is the same for all electromagnetic waves travelling in a vacuum?
A frequency
B wavelength
C speed
D amplitude
parts.answer: C speed
parts.working: All electromagnetic waves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. Frequency and wavelength differ across the spectrum, so A and B are wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum used in each case: (i) a thermal-imaging camera, (ii) checking for forged banknotes, (iii) seeing a broken bone, (iv) killing cancer cells, (v) mobile-phone calls.
parts.answer: (i) infrared (ii) ultraviolet (iii) X-rays (iv) gamma rays (X-rays also accepted) (v) microwaves (radio waves also accepted)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one harmful effect on the human body of each of: (i) microwaves, (ii) infrared, (iii) ultraviolet, (iv) gamma rays.
parts.answer: (i) internal heating of body tissue (ii) skin burns (iii) damage to skin cells leading to skin cancer / damage to eyes (iv) mutation of cells / cancer

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two properties shared by all electromagnetic waves.
parts.answer: They are transverse; travel at the same speed (3.0 × 10⁸ m/s) in a vacuum; can travel through a vacuum; transfer energy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An AM radio station broadcasts at 1.5 MHz. Calculate the wavelength of the radio waves.

practice.stem: A café in Islamabad has a Wi-Fi router transmitting at 2.4 GHz and a radio tuned to an FM station at 101 MHz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the speed of electromagnetic waves in air.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the Wi-Fi signal.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the FM radio signal.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the region of the electromagnetic spectrum to which each signal belongs.
parts.answer: Wi-Fi: microwaves; FM radio: radio waves.

practice.stem: The speed of electromagnetic waves is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Light from the Sun travels 1.5 × 10¹¹ m to the Earth. Calculate the time taken in seconds.
parts.working: M1 t = d ÷ v; A1 500 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: A radio signal is sent from Earth to a spacecraft near the Moon, 3.84 × 10⁸ m away, and a reply is sent straight back. Calculate the total time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one problem this delay would cause for an engineer steering a robot rover on the Moon from Earth.
parts.answer: The engineer sees what the rover did 1.28 s ago and the command arrives late, so it may hit obstacles before reacting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of a microwave signal of wavelength 0.125 m.
parts.working: M1 f = c ÷ λ; A1 2.4 × 10⁹ Hz

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why microwaves are used for satellite TV signals.
parts.answer: They pass through the atmosphere (and the ionosphere) without being reflected or absorbed much.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A microwave oven also uses microwaves. Explain why the food gets hot.
parts.answer: Water molecules in the food absorb the microwave energy; they vibrate more, so the internal energy and temperature of the food rise.
parts.working: B1 microwaves absorbed by water in food; B1 increased kinetic energy of molecules / heating

parts.label: a
parts.text: After an earthquake, rescue teams use thermal-imaging cameras to find people trapped under rubble. Explain how this works.
parts.answer: All warm objects emit infrared; a living person is warmer than the rubble, so emits more infrared, which the camera detects and shows as a bright area.
parts.working: B1 body emits infrared; B1 warmer than surroundings so shows up

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other uses of infrared radiation.
parts.answer: Television remote controls; grills/toasters; optical-fibre communication; intruder alarms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why bones show clearly on an X-ray image.
parts.answer: Bone absorbs X-rays much more than soft tissue, so fewer X-rays reach the detector behind bone, giving a pale shadow.
parts.working: B1 bone absorbs, soft tissue lets through; B1 contrast on detector

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two precautions taken by a radiographer who takes many X-ray images every day.
parts.answer: Stands behind a lead screen or leaves the room; wears a film badge/dosimeter; uses the lowest exposure; lead apron.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the patient is not harmed much by one X-ray image.
parts.answer: The exposure is very short and the dose is small.

practice.stem: A Pakistani television channel broadcasts live cricket using a communications satellite in a geostationary orbit about 36 000 km above the Equator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why microwaves, rather than visible light or long-wave radio, are used to communicate with satellites.
parts.answer: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere (and clouds) without much absorption, and their short wavelength means little diffraction, so they can be sent as a narrow beam to the satellite.
parts.working: B1 pass through atmosphere/ionosphere; B1 little diffraction / narrow beam (or high data rate).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for a signal to travel from a ground station up to the satellite and back down to a receiver directly below. Assume the satellite is 36 000 km above both.
parts.working: C1 distance = 2 × 3.6 × 10⁷ m; C1 t = d ÷ v; A1 0.24 s.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A television's remote control uses a different region of the spectrum. Name it and state one reason why it is suitable.
parts.answer: Infrared; it is short range, does not pass through walls (no interference with neighbours), and is harmless at low power.
parts.working: B1 infrared; B1 any suitable reason.

practice.stem: The speed of electromagnetic waves is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each frequency, calculate the wavelength and name the region of the spectrum: 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz, 1.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz, 1.0 × 10¹³ Hz, 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz, 1.0 × 10¹⁶ Hz, 1.0 × 10¹⁸ Hz.
parts.answer: 3.0 m radio; 0.030 m microwaves; 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m infrared; 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m visible light; 3.0 × 10⁻⁸ m ultraviolet; 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m X-rays
parts.working: M1 λ = c ÷ f; A2 all six wavelengths correct (A1 for three or four correct); B1 radio and microwave named; B1 infrared and visible named; B1 ultraviolet and X-rays named

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the energy carried by the waves changes as the frequency increases, and give one consequence for safety.
parts.answer: Higher frequency waves are more energetic/more ionising, so ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are more dangerous to living cells.
parts.working: B1 more dangerous / ionising at higher frequency; B1 consequence

practice.stem: The speed of electromagnetic waves is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An airport radar sends a microwave pulse which returns from an aircraft 0.20 ms later. Calculate the distance to the aircraft in km.
parts.answer: 30 km

parts.label: b
parts.text: A second pulse, sent 10 s later, returns after 0.18 ms. Calculate the average speed of the aircraft towards the radar.
parts.working: M1 new distance = 27 km; M1 change 3.0 km in 10 s; A1 300 m/s

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why microwaves rather than visible light are used for air-traffic radar.
parts.answer: Microwaves pass through cloud, rain and fog, which scatter or block visible light.

practice.stem: The speed of electromagnetic waves is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A satellite-navigation (GPS) satellite is 20 200 km from a receiver. Calculate the time taken for its radio signal to reach the receiver.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The receiver works out its distance from the travel time. Calculate the error in distance if the time is measured 1.0 µs too long.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to explain why satellite-navigation systems need extremely accurate clocks.
parts.answer: Even a tiny timing error gives a large error in position because the waves travel so fast.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes the particles in a liquid?
A They are far apart and move freely at high speed.
B They are close together and vibrate about fixed positions only.
C They are close together and move around each other at random.
D They are far apart and vibrate about fixed positions.
parts.answer: C They are close together and move around each other at random.
parts.working: Liquid particles are close together (liquids are hard to compress) but are not in fixed positions, so they slide past each other at random. B describes a solid; A describes a gas.

practice.stem: A student in a school laboratory in Peshawar fills a small glass cell with smoke and lights it from the side. She looks at the cell through a microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the motion of the bright specks of smoke seen through the microscope.
parts.answer: Random / zig-zag / jerky movement in all directions, constantly changing direction.
parts.working: B1 random or zig-zag; B1 continual changes of direction (not just 'they move').

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what causes this motion.
parts.answer: Air molecules (too small to be seen) move fast and randomly; they collide with the much larger smoke particles; the collisions are uneven from different sides, giving an unbalanced force that changes at random.
parts.working: B1 air molecules move randomly at high speed; B1 they collide with / bombard the smoke particles; B1 unequal numbers/forces of collisions on different sides at any instant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what this observation suggests about the speed of the air molecules compared with the speed of the smoke particles.
parts.answer: The air molecules move much faster (they are much lighter than the smoke particles).

practice.stem: A delivery rider in Lahore checks the air in his motorcycle tyre before a long ride.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the air molecules, how the air inside the tyre exerts a pressure on the tyre wall.
parts.answer: Molecules move randomly at high speed; they collide with the wall and rebound; each collision changes the molecule's momentum, so a force acts on the wall; force per unit area is the pressure.
parts.working: B1 molecules hit the walls; B1 change of momentum / rebound gives a force on the wall; B1 pressure = force ÷ area (many collisions over the area).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rider pumps more air into the tyre. Its volume and temperature do not change. Explain why the pressure increases.
parts.answer: More molecules in the same volume, so more collisions with each unit area of wall per second, so a larger force per unit area.
parts.working: B1 more molecules (per unit volume); B1 more frequent collisions with the wall → greater force per unit area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between evaporation and boiling.
parts.answer: Evaporation happens at any temperature; boiling only at the boiling point. Evaporation happens only at the surface; boiling happens throughout the liquid (bubbles form).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: any temperature vs fixed temperature (boiling point); surface only vs throughout the liquid; no bubbles vs bubbles; evaporation causes cooling of the liquid while boiling needs continuous heating at constant temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On a hot day a cricketer sweats. Explain, in terms of molecules, why the evaporation of sweat cools his skin.
parts.answer: The most energetic (fastest) water molecules escape from the surface; the molecules left behind have a lower average kinetic energy; so the temperature of the remaining sweat falls and it takes thermal energy from the skin.
parts.working: B1 more energetic / faster molecules escape from the surface; B1 average kinetic energy of remaining molecules decreases; B1 so temperature of the liquid (and skin) falls / energy drawn from the skin.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The temperature of a gas in a sealed container rises. What happens to the gas molecules?
A They get bigger.
B Their average speed increases.
C They move closer together.
D The number of molecules increases.
parts.answer: B Their average speed increases.
parts.working: Temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so they move faster on average. A is a common misconception: the molecules themselves do not expand; and in a sealed container their number and spacing do not change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the arrangement and motion of the particles in (i) a solid, (ii) a liquid, (iii) a gas.
parts.answer: (i) close together in a regular pattern, vibrating about fixed positions; (ii) close together, irregular, moving around (sliding past) each other; (iii) far apart, random, moving quickly in all directions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a gas can be squashed (compressed) easily but a liquid cannot.
parts.answer: Gas particles are far apart with large spaces between them that can be reduced; liquid particles are already touching (close together).
parts.working: B1 gas: large spaces; B1 liquid: particles close together, little space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A balloon is blown up in a warm room and then put into a freezer. After a while it has become smaller. Explain, in terms of the air molecules, why it shrinks.
parts.answer: The molecules lose kinetic energy and move more slowly; they hit the inside of the balloon less often and with smaller force, so the pressure inside falls; the balloon contracts until the pressures inside and outside balance.
parts.working: B1 molecules slower; B1 fewer / weaker collisions with the wall; B1 lower pressure so volume decreases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the balloon when it is taken out of the freezer.
parts.answer: It expands back towards its original size as the air warms.

practice.stem: A sealed plastic syringe contains 60 cm³ of air at a pressure of 100 kPa. The plunger is pushed in slowly until the volume of the air is 24 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new pressure of the air.
parts.answer: 250 kPa
parts.working: C1 p₁V₁ = p₂V₂; C1 100 × 60 = p₂ × 24; A1 p₂ = 250 kPa.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one assumption you made in (a).
parts.answer: The temperature of the air stays constant (and no air escapes).
parts.working: B1 constant temperature or fixed mass of gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of molecules, why the pressure increases when the volume is reduced.
parts.answer: The same number of molecules are in a smaller volume, so they hit each unit area of the walls more often; greater force per unit area.
parts.working: B1 molecules closer together / more per unit volume; B1 more frequent collisions with the walls (per unit area).

practice.stem: A sealed metal flask of fixed volume contains air. The flask is placed in a water bath and heated slowly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the gas molecules, why the pressure in the flask increases as it is heated.
parts.answer: The molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster; they hit the walls more often and with greater force (greater change of momentum); so the force per unit area on the walls increases.
parts.working: B1 molecules move faster / more kinetic energy; B1 more frequent collisions with walls; B1 harder collisions / greater change of momentum, so greater force per unit area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The room temperature is 20 °C. Convert this temperature to kelvin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by absolute zero and give its value in °C.
parts.answer: The lowest possible temperature, at which the particles have the least possible kinetic energy; −273 °C (0 K).
parts.working: B1 lowest possible temperature / particles have least kinetic energy; B1 −273 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A fixed mass of gas has a volume of 3.0 m³ at a pressure of 120 kPa. The pressure is increased to 180 kPa at constant temperature. What is the new volume?
A 1.5 m³
B 2.0 m³
C 4.5 m³
D 7.2 m³
parts.answer: B 2.0 m³
parts.working: pV = constant: 120 × 3.0 = 180 × V, so V = 2.0 m³. C (4.5 m³) comes from multiplying by 180/120 instead of dividing.

practice.stem: In many homes in Sindh, drinking water is stored in an unglazed clay pot called a matka. The clay has tiny pores, so the outside of the pot is always slightly damp.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the water inside the matka becomes cooler than the surrounding air.
parts.answer: Water seeps through the pores and evaporates from the outer surface; the most energetic molecules escape; the average kinetic energy of the remaining water falls, so it cools and draws thermal energy from the water inside.
parts.working: B1 water evaporates from outer surface; B1 faster/more energetic molecules escape; B1 average KE (temperature) of remaining water decreases / energy taken from water inside.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the family could make the water cool faster. Give a reason for each.
parts.answer: Place the matka in a breeze / near a fan – moving air carries away water vapour so more molecules escape; place it where the air is dry (low humidity) – vapour does not return to the surface; use a matka with a larger surface area – more molecules at the surface can escape.
parts.working: For each of two ways: B1 way, B1 matching reason. Accept draught/wind, larger surface area, drier air, higher outside temperature (with reason).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The matka works less well during the humid monsoon season. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The air already contains a lot of water vapour, so the rate of evaporation is lower.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Wet clothes are hung out to dry. Which change does NOT increase the rate at which the water evaporates?
A raising the air temperature
B spreading the clothes out to increase their surface area
C a wind blowing across the clothes
D an increase in the humidity of the air
parts.answer: D an increase in the humidity of the air
parts.working: Humid air already contains much water vapour, so more molecules return to the cloth and evaporation slows. A, B and C all increase the rate (more energetic molecules, more surface molecules, vapour carried away).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Liquid nitrogen boils at −196 °C. Convert this temperature into kelvin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert 300 K into °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the kelvin temperature of a gas and the average kinetic energy of its molecules.
parts.answer: The average kinetic energy is (directly) proportional to the kelvin temperature: the higher the temperature, the greater the average kinetic energy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what is meant by absolute zero in terms of molecular motion.
parts.answer: The temperature at which the particles have the least possible kinetic energy (they have the least possible motion).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two identical thermometers hang side by side. The bulb of one is wrapped in a cloth kept wet with water. Explain why the wet thermometer shows a lower temperature.
parts.answer: Water evaporates from the cloth; the more energetic (faster) molecules escape from the surface; the average kinetic energy of those left falls, so the water, and the bulb, cool.
parts.working: B1 evaporation; B1 most energetic molecules escape; B1 average KE of remaining molecules decreases so temperature falls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The difference between the two readings is larger in dry Quetta than in humid Karachi. Explain why.
parts.answer: In dry air evaporation is faster, so the cooling is greater; in humid air many water molecules return to the cloth, so evaporation and cooling are slower.
parts.working: B1 faster evaporation in dry air; B1 slower in humid air because of vapour already present.

practice.stem:
A student investigates how the pressure p of a fixed mass of air depends on its volume V. The air is trapped in a sealed tube connected to a pressure gauge. She changes the volume, waits one minute, then reads the gauge. Results:
V / cm³: 50.0, 40.0, 30.0, 25.0, 20.0
p / kPa: 102, 128, 150, 204, 255

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate p × V for each reading.
parts.working: B2 all five correct; B1 for three or four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the anomalous reading and suggest one cause.
parts.answer: The reading at 30.0 cm³ (150 kPa) – pV is about 4500 instead of about 5100. Cause: the gauge was read before the gas returned to room temperature, or the gauge/volume was misread (it should be about 170 kPa).
parts.working: B1 identifies 30.0 cm³ reading; B1 sensible cause (misreading scale, gas temperature not constant / reading too soon, parallax at scale).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the results support the relationship p ∝ 1/V. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Yes – apart from the anomalous point, p × V is constant (5100–5120, within 1 %), so p is inversely proportional to V.
parts.working: B1 yes; B1 reason: pV constant for the other readings (within experimental error).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the student waited one minute after each change of volume before reading the pressure.
parts.answer: Compressing the gas warms it; waiting lets it return to room temperature so the temperature is constant.

practice.stem: A diver near Astola Island breathes out an air bubble at a depth where the total pressure is 250 kPa. The bubble has a volume of 1.2 cm³. At the surface the pressure is 100 kPa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the bubble at the surface. Assume its temperature does not change.
parts.answer: 3.0 cm³
parts.working: C1 p₁V₁ = p₂V₂; C1 250 × 1.2 = 100 × V; A1 3.0 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of molecules, why the bubble expands as it rises.
parts.answer: The water pressure outside the bubble decreases as depth decreases; the gas molecules inside now exert a greater pressure than the water pushing in, so the bubble grows; as the volume increases, collisions per unit area become less frequent until the gas pressure equals the outside pressure.
parts.working: B1 outside pressure falls as it rises; B1 molecules' collisions push the bubble wall outwards (gas pressure > outside); B1 larger volume → fewer collisions per unit area until pressures balance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Divers are trained never to hold their breath while rising quickly to the surface. Use your answer to (a) to suggest why.
parts.answer: The air in the lungs would expand (about 2.5 times here) and could damage the lungs.

practice.stem: An aerosol can of air freshener carries the warning: 'Do not expose to temperatures above 50 °C.' On a summer afternoon in Jacobabad the inside of a parked car rises from 25 °C to 60 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert 25 °C and 60 °C to kelvin.
parts.answer: 298 K and 333 K

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the molecules of gas inside the can, why the can could burst if it is left in a hot car.
parts.answer: Temperature rise increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules; they hit the walls more often and harder; volume is fixed, so the pressure rises until it may exceed the strength of the can.
parts.working: B1 molecules move faster / greater average KE; B1 more frequent and harder collisions (greater change of momentum per collision); B1 volume fixed so pressure increases (can bursts).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says: 'The kelvin temperature has nearly doubled, so the pressure has nearly doubled.' Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: The kelvin temperature only rises from 298 K to 333 K, about 12 %; it is the Celsius value that has more than doubled, so the pressure rises by a much smaller fraction.
parts.working: B1 kelvin values 298 → 333 K (not doubled); B1 so increase in pressure is small (about 12 %) / Celsius doubling is not meaningful because 0 °C is not absolute zero.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why there is a lowest possible temperature.
parts.answer: Temperature depends on the kinetic energy of particles; at absolute zero the particles have the least possible kinetic energy and cannot lose any more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas cylinder used for welding has a volume of 0.050 m³ and contains gas at a pressure of 1.2 × 10⁷ Pa. Calculate the volume this gas would occupy at atmospheric pressure, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, at the same temperature.
parts.answer: 6.0 m³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas is used to fill balloons, each of volume 0.50 m³ at atmospheric pressure. Calculate how many balloons can be completely filled. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 11; 0.050 m³ of gas at atmospheric pressure stays in the cylinder, so 5.95 m³ is available, enough for 11.9 balloons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made in your calculations.
parts.answer: The temperature of the gas stays constant (fixed mass of gas).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An air bubble of volume 2.0 cm³ forms at the bottom of a lake, where the pressure is 150 kPa. The bubble rises slowly to the surface, where the pressure is 100 kPa. Assume the temperature of the bubble stays constant. Calculate the volume of the bubble at the surface.
parts.answer: 3.0 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: The pressure on the bubble at depth h is the surface pressure plus ρgh. Calculate the depth of the bubble when the pressure on it is 150 kPa, given that the pressure at the surface is 100 kPa. Water density = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of molecules, why the bubble gets bigger as it rises.
parts.answer: The pressure of the water outside falls as the bubble rises, so the gas inside expands. The molecules are then spread over a larger volume, so they hit the surface less often for each unit area, balancing the lower outside pressure.
parts.working: B1 outside pressure decreases, so the gas expands; B1 same number of molecules in a larger volume, so fewer collisions per unit area and lower pressure inside, matching the outside.

practice.stem:
A student traps a fixed mass of air in a gas syringe. The nozzle is sealed and the plunger is free to move, so the pressure of the air stays at atmospheric pressure. The syringe is placed in water baths at different temperatures θ, and the volume V of the air is read from the scale once each reading has settled.
θ / °C: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80
V / cm³: 73.2, 78.5, 83.9, 89.2, 94.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert each temperature into kelvin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate V ÷ T for each reading, where T is the kelvin temperature. Give each value to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.268 cm³/K for every reading
parts.working: M1 dividing each volume by its kelvin temperature; A1 all five values are 0.268 cm³/K.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conclusion that can be drawn from your results.
parts.answer: At constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its kelvin temperature.
parts.working: B1 volume proportional to kelvin temperature (Charles's law).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict the volume of the air at 100 °C.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain, in terms of molecules, why the volume increases as the air is heated at constant pressure.
parts.answer: The molecules move faster, so they hit the plunger harder and more often; to keep the pressure equal to atmospheric pressure the plunger moves out and the air expands.
parts.working: B1 faster molecules give more frequent and harder collisions with the plunger (higher pressure); B1 plunger moves out so the pressure stays at atmospheric, giving a larger volume.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Water boils at 100 °C at normal atmospheric pressure. What is this temperature in kelvin?
A −173 K
B 100 K
C 273 K
D 373 K
parts.answer: D 373 K
parts.working: T (K) = θ (°C) + 273 = 100 + 273 = 373 K. 273 K is the melting point of ice, not the boiling point.

practice.stem: Overhead power cables between pylons near Multan are hung so that they sag slightly. In summer the afternoon temperature can reach 48 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why the cables sag more on a hot afternoon.
parts.answer: The particles in the metal gain energy and vibrate more (with larger amplitude); they push further apart, so the cable expands / gets longer and sags more.
parts.working: B1 particles vibrate more / faster; B1 average separation increases so the cable gets longer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why engineers do not hang the cables tight in winter.
parts.answer: In cold weather the cable contracts; if it were tight it could snap or pull the pylons together.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Equal volumes of a solid, a liquid and a gas are heated through the same temperature rise. State which expands the most and which expands the least.
parts.answer: Gas expands most; solid expands least.
parts.working: B1 gas most; B1 solid least.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define specific heat capacity.
parts.answer: The energy needed per unit mass to raise the temperature by one degree (1 °C or 1 K).
parts.working: B1 energy per unit mass (per kg); B1 per degree rise in temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of 2.0 kg of water by 35 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/(kg °C).

practice.stem: A block of ice taken from a freezer at −18 °C is heated steadily until it has all melted and the water is at 30 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the temperature of the substance while it is melting.
parts.answer: It stays constant (at the melting point).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why energy must still be supplied while the substance melts.
parts.answer: The energy is used to break/weaken the forces (bonds) between particles so they can move past each other; it does not increase their kinetic energy, so temperature does not rise.
parts.working: B1 energy breaks / overcomes forces of attraction between particles; B1 kinetic energy (temperature) does not increase.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define specific latent heat of fusion.
parts.answer: The energy needed to change unit mass of a substance from solid to liquid without any change in temperature.
parts.working: B1 energy per unit mass to change solid to liquid; B1 at constant temperature / no temperature change.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why are small gaps left between the ends of steel railway rails when they are laid?
A to allow the rails to expand in hot weather
B to let rainwater drain away
C to reduce friction on the train wheels
D to allow the rails to contract in hot weather
parts.answer: A to allow the rails to expand in hot weather
parts.working: Steel expands when its temperature rises; without gaps the rails would push against each other and buckle. D is wrong because solids expand, not contract, when heated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An iron cooking pot of mass 2.0 kg is heated from 25 °C to 75 °C. The specific heat capacity of iron is 450 J/(kg °C). Calculate the energy needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An aluminium pot of the same mass is heated through the same temperature rise. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/(kg °C). Calculate the energy needed and state why it is more.
parts.answer: 90 000 J; aluminium needs more energy per kilogram for each degree (larger specific heat capacity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the change of state when (i) a liquid becomes a gas at its boiling point, (ii) a gas becomes a liquid, (iii) a liquid becomes a solid.
parts.answer: (i) boiling; (ii) condensation; (iii) solidification (freezing)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A burn from steam at 100 °C is usually much worse than a burn from the same mass of water at 100 °C. Explain why.
parts.answer: When steam condenses on the skin it releases its latent heat of vaporisation, a large amount of extra energy, before cooling like the water.
parts.working: B1 condensation releases latent heat; B1 so more energy is given to the skin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Normal body temperature is 37 °C. Convert this into kelvin.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The temperature at night on a high mountain is 250 K. Convert this into °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the internal energy of an object when its temperature rises.
parts.answer: It increases.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe, in terms of particles, what happens when the temperature of a solid rises.
parts.answer: The particles vibrate faster / with more kinetic energy.

practice.stem: An electric kettle has a power of 2200 W. It contains 1.5 kg of water at 25 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/(kg °C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy needed to heat the water to 100 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum time this takes.
parts.answer: 215 s (about 3.6 minutes)
parts.working: C1 t = E ÷ P; A1 215 s (ecf from a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The actual time is longer. Suggest two reasons.
parts.answer: Thermal energy is lost from the kettle to the surroundings; energy is also needed to heat the kettle itself (and the element).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: energy lost to the air/surroundings; energy heats the kettle body and element; some water evaporates; supply voltage lower than rated.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Blocks of aluminium and copper have the same mass. Each receives the same quantity of thermal energy. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/(kg °C) and that of copper is 390 J/(kg °C). Which statement is correct?
A Both blocks have the same temperature rise.
B The aluminium block has about 2.3 times the temperature rise of the copper block.
C The copper block has about 2.3 times the temperature rise of the aluminium block.
D The copper block has about 0.43 times the temperature rise of the aluminium block.
parts.answer: C The copper block has about 2.3 times the temperature rise of the aluminium block.
parts.working: Δθ = E ÷ (mc); with E and m equal, Δθ ∝ 1/c, so Δθ(Cu)/Δθ(Al) = 900/390 ≈ 2.3. B reverses the ratio.

practice.stem: Water in a kettle is already boiling. The kettle stands on a balance. The 2000 W heater is left on for 100 s and the reading on the balance falls by 0.090 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy supplied by the heater in 100 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate a value for the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the temperature of the water stays at 100 °C even though the heater is still switched on.
parts.answer: The energy supplied is used to separate the molecules / overcome the forces between them (change of state to steam), not to increase their kinetic energy.
parts.working: B1 energy used to overcome intermolecular forces / change state; B1 average kinetic energy of molecules does not increase.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest whether your answer to (b) is likely to be greater or smaller than the true value. Explain.
parts.answer: Greater – some of the heater's energy is lost to the surroundings, so less than 200 000 J actually boils the 0.090 kg of water.
parts.working: B1 greater; B1 energy lost to surroundings so the energy used for vaporisation is overestimated.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg. How much energy is needed to melt 0.50 kg of ice at 0 °C?
A 1.67 × 10² J
B 1.67 × 10⁵ J
C 3.34 × 10⁵ J
D 6.68 × 10⁵ J
parts.working: E = mL = 0.50 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 1.67 × 10⁵ J. D divides by the mass instead of multiplying.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A steam iron turns 0.030 kg of water at 100 °C into steam every minute. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg. Calculate the energy needed each minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the minimum power of the heater in the iron needed for this.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the temperature of the boiling water does not rise even though the heater is on.
parts.answer: The energy is used to break the bonds (forces of attraction) between molecules so they can separate, not to increase their kinetic energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fire alarm contains a bimetallic strip made of brass bonded to steel. Brass expands more than steel for the same temperature rise. Describe what happens to the strip when it is heated.
parts.answer: It bends (curves), with the brass on the outside of the curve.
parts.working: B1 bends; B1 brass on the outside (longer side).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this can make the alarm ring.
parts.answer: The bending strip touches a contact and completes an electric circuit to the bell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why solids expand when heated.
parts.answer: The particles vibrate with greater amplitude (more kinetic energy), so on average they move slightly further apart.
parts.working: B1 vibrate more; B1 further apart.

practice.stem:
A cook in a café in Islamabad mixes 0.3 kg of water at 80 °C with 0.2 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated jug. She then adds 0.05 kg of ice at 0 °C.
Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg °C); specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the temperature of the mixture is 56 °C. Assume no energy is lost to the surroundings or the jug.
parts.working: M1 energy lost by hot water = energy gained by cold: 0.30 × c × (80 − T) = 0.20 × c × (T − 20); A1 T = 56 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the final temperature after the ice has melted and the water has mixed. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: C1 energy to melt ice = 0.050 × 3.34 × 10⁵ = 16 700 J; C1 energy from warm water = 0.50 × 4200 × (56 − T); C1 energy to warm melted ice = 0.050 × 4200 × (T − 0); A1 T = 43.7 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a cube of ice at 0 °C cools a drink more than the same mass of water at 0 °C.
parts.answer: The ice must first absorb latent heat to melt (without changing temperature); this extra energy is taken from the drink before the melted water then warms up.
parts.working: B1 ice absorbs latent heat of fusion to melt; B1 so more energy is removed from the drink.

practice.stem:
A student finds the specific heat capacity of aluminium. A 1.00 kg aluminium block has two holes: one for a 12 V heater and one for a thermometer. The heater current is 4.0 A. The heater is switched on for 300 s.
Temperature at start = 22.0 °C; highest temperature = 37.5 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the electrical energy supplied by the heater.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium given by these results.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The accepted value is 900 J/(kg °C). State whether the student's value agrees with it within 10 %. Show your working.
parts.answer: Yes – it is about 3.2 % larger, which is within 10 %.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to the experiment, explaining how each improves the result.
parts.answer: Wrap the block in insulation (e.g. cotton wool / foam) to reduce energy losses to the surroundings; put a few drops of oil in the thermometer hole for good thermal contact; start from a block cooled a few degrees below room temperature and heat to the same amount above it, so gains and losses balance; use a thermometer with a finer scale (or a digital one) for more precise readings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two improvements with reasons, tied to this apparatus.

practice.stem:
A boiling tube of a waxy substance X is melted in hot water, then removed and allowed to cool in air. A student records its temperature every minute:
time / min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8
temperature / °C: 80.0, 74.0, 69.5, 69.0, 69.0, 69.0, 68.5, 62.0, 56.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the freezing point of substance X shown by these results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the results show that X is changing state between 3 min and 6 min.
parts.answer: The temperature stays (almost) constant while the substance is still losing energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why the temperature stays constant while X freezes even though it is losing energy to the surroundings.
parts.answer: As particles form bonds / become fixed in a lattice, energy (latent heat) is released; this replaces the energy lost to the surroundings so the average kinetic energy does not fall.
parts.working: B1 bonds form between particles / latent heat released; B1 balances energy lost, so kinetic energy / temperature unchanged.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of cooling, in °C/min, of the liquid between 0 and 2 min and of the solid between 7 and 8 min.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest why taking a reading every 30 s, instead of every minute, would give a more reliable freezing point.
parts.answer: More readings during the flat part, so the constant temperature is identified more clearly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gas water heater (geyser) heats 120 kg of water from 15 °C to 60 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/(kg °C). Calculate the energy given to the water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The heater is 75 % efficient. Calculate the energy released by the burning gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each kilogram of gas releases 5.0 × 10⁷ J. Calculate the mass of gas burnt.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way of increasing the efficiency of the heater.
parts.answer: Insulate the tank and pipes (or reduce energy carried away by the hot flue gases).

practice.stem: To find the specific heat capacity of brass, a student heats a 0.20 kg brass block in boiling water at 100 °C. She quickly moves it into 0.15 kg of water at 20.0 °C in an insulated cup and stirs. The highest temperature reached is 28.5 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/(kg °C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy gained by the water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assuming all this energy came from the brass, calculate the specific heat capacity of brass.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student's value is likely to be lower than the true value.
parts.answer: Some energy is lost from the brass while it is moved (so its temperature fall is less than 71.5 °C), and some energy from the water is lost to the cup and air; both make the calculated c too small.
parts.working: B1 energy lost during transfer / to surroundings; B1 linked to smaller calculated value.

practice.stem: A 500 W heater is placed in 0.80 kg of solid wax. The temperature rises to 60 °C after 4.0 minutes, stays at 60 °C until 10.0 minutes, and then rises again, reaching 80 °C 80 s later. Assume all the energy from the heater goes into the wax.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the melting point of the wax.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the specific latent heat of fusion of the wax.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the specific heat capacity of the liquid wax.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why, in practice, the true value of the specific latent heat is smaller than your answer to (b).
parts.answer: Some of the heater's energy is lost to the surroundings, so less than 180 000 J actually melts the wax.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Thermal energy reaches the Earth from the Sun through space. Which method of transfer is this?
A conduction
B convection
C evaporation
D infrared radiation
parts.answer: D infrared radiation
parts.working: Space is (almost) a vacuum, and only electromagnetic radiation travels without a medium. Conduction and convection need particles.

practice.stem: A karahi (cooking wok) is made of steel, but its two handles are made of wood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the metal body of the karahi is a good choice for cooking.
parts.answer: Metal is a good thermal conductor, so energy passes quickly from the flame to the food.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, how thermal energy is conducted through the metal.
parts.answer: Particles (atoms/ions) at the hot side vibrate more and pass energy to neighbouring particles through collisions/bonds; metals also have free (delocalised) electrons that gain kinetic energy and move quickly through the metal, carrying energy to cooler parts.
parts.working: B1 atoms/lattice vibrations passed to neighbours; B1 free/delocalised electrons; B1 electrons move through the metal and transfer energy by collisions (faster than lattice alone).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the handles are made of wood.
parts.answer: Wood is a poor conductor (insulator), so the handles stay cool enough to hold.

practice.stem: In a flat in Karachi, a split air conditioner is fixed high up on the wall near the ceiling.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the air conditioner is mounted high on the wall.
parts.answer: The cold air from the unit is denser than the warm air in the room; it sinks; warm, less dense air rises to the top to be cooled, setting up a convection current that cools the whole room.
parts.working: B1 cold air is more dense; B1 cold air sinks / warm air rises; B1 convection current circulates air through the whole room.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In winter the family uses a gas heater. State where in the room the heater should be placed and explain why.
parts.answer: Near the floor – the warm air it produces is less dense and rises, so a convection current carries warm air around the room.
parts.working: B1 low down / at floor level; B1 hot air rises (less dense) to set up a convection current.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does a woollen jumper keep a person warm in winter?
A Wool traps air, which is a poor conductor of thermal energy.
B Wool is a good conductor of thermal energy.
C Wool reflects all the infrared radiation from the body.
D Wool stops cold from entering the body.
parts.answer: A Wool traps air, which is a poor conductor of thermal energy.
parts.working: Still air trapped between the fibres is a poor conductor and cannot form convection currents, so energy loss from the body is reduced. D is a misconception: 'cold' is not transferred; thermal energy flows out of the warm body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A family in Quetta wants to keep its house warm in winter. Explain how double glazing reduces thermal energy loss through the windows.
parts.answer: The two panes are separated by a layer of air (or vacuum), which is a poor conductor; the gap is narrow so convection is reduced.
parts.working: B1 trapped air / vacuum poor conductor; B1 little convection in the narrow gap.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a layer of fibreglass in the roof space reduces thermal energy loss.
parts.answer: Fibreglass traps air in small pockets; air is a poor conductor and cannot move to form convection currents.
parts.working: B1 traps air, poor conductor; B1 prevents convection.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one other way the family can reduce thermal energy loss.
parts.answer: Any one: thick curtains; draught excluders / sealing gaps; carpets; insulating walls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many houses in Sindh are painted white on the outside. Explain how this helps to keep them cool in summer.
parts.answer: White surfaces are poor absorbers (good reflectors) of radiation, so less of the Sun's energy is absorbed.
parts.working: B1 white reflects; B1 absorbs less energy from the Sun.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Black car seats get much hotter than light-coloured seats in sunshine. Explain why.
