parts.answer: Dull black surfaces are good absorbers of infrared and visible radiation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the method of thermal energy transfer from the Sun to the car.
parts.answer: (infrared) radiation

parts.label: a
parts.text: On a cold morning a metal bench and a wooden bench in a park are at the same temperature. Explain why the metal bench feels colder to sit on.
parts.answer: Metal is a good conductor, so it conducts thermal energy away from the body quickly; wood is a poor conductor (insulator).
parts.working: B1 metal good conductor; B1 energy taken from body faster.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a material that is a poor conductor and give one use of it in the home.
parts.answer: e.g. plastic for pan handles / wood / air in insulation / polystyrene.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four identical metal cans are filled with the same volume of water at 90 °C. Each can has a different outer surface. Which can cools fastest?
A dull black
B shiny black
C dull white
D shiny silver
parts.answer: A dull black
parts.working: Dull black surfaces are the best emitters of infrared radiation, so that can loses energy fastest. Shiny silver is the poorest emitter.

practice.stem:
A student tests how the colour of a surface affects the rate of cooling. Two identical aluminium cans with lids are used: one painted dull black and one polished shiny silver. Each is filled with 250 cm³ of water at 80.0 °C and left on a wooden bench. After 15 minutes:
dull black can: 61.5 °C
shiny silver can: 70.0 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature drop of each can.
parts.answer: Black: 18.5 °C; silver: 10.0 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the results show about the two surfaces.
parts.answer: The dull black surface is the better emitter of infrared radiation (it cooled more).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State three variables that must be kept the same for this to be a fair test.
parts.answer: Volume/mass of water; starting temperature; size/shape/material of can; time of cooling; room temperature / draughts; both with lids (or both without).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why both cans were fitted with lids made of the same material.
parts.answer: To reduce (and keep equal) energy loss by evaporation and convection from the water surface, so the difference is due to the can surfaces.

practice.stem: A vacuum flask keeps tea hot during a family trip to Murree. It has a double-walled glass container with a vacuum between the walls. The glass surfaces facing the vacuum are silvered. The flask is closed with a hollow plastic stopper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the vacuum between the two glass walls reduces thermal energy transfer.
parts.answer: Conduction and convection need particles; a vacuum has no particles, so neither can occur across the gap.
parts.working: B1 no particles / medium in vacuum; B1 so no conduction or convection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the silvered surfaces reduce thermal energy transfer.
parts.answer: Shiny surfaces are poor emitters of infrared radiation and good reflectors, so radiation from the hot tea is reflected back and little is emitted across the gap.
parts.working: B1 poor emitter; B1 reflects infrared back towards the liquid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the stopper is made of hollow plastic.
parts.answer: Plastic is a poor conductor, and the trapped air in the hollow is also a poor conductor; the stopper also stops convection currents and evaporation from the top.
parts.working: B1 poor conductor (plastic/trapped air); B1 prevents convection / evaporation losses from the top.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of radiation that the Earth's surface mainly emits.
parts.answer: Infrared radiation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the average temperature of the Earth stays roughly constant over many years.
parts.answer: The Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun and emits infrared radiation into space; when the rate of absorbing equals the rate of emitting, the temperature stays constant.
parts.working: B1 absorbs from Sun and emits infrared; B1 rates of absorption and emission are equal (balance).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide absorb some of the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth. Explain why an increase in these gases causes the Earth's average temperature to rise.
parts.answer: Less infrared escapes into space, so the rate of energy loss falls below the rate of absorption; the Earth warms; as it warms it emits more until a new balance is reached at a higher temperature.
parts.working: B1 less radiation escapes; B1 energy in > energy out so temperature rises; B1 new balance at higher temperature (hotter body emits more).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which situation is convection the main method of thermal energy transfer?
A energy passing through the steel base of a cooking pan
B water in an electric kettle being heated by an element at the bottom
C warmth felt on the face from a bonfire several metres away
D energy from the Sun reaching the Earth
parts.answer: B water in an electric kettle being heated by an element at the bottom
parts.working: Water heated at the bottom expands, becomes less dense and rises, setting up a convection current. A is conduction; C and D are infrared radiation.

practice.stem:
A student compares how well four metal rods conduct thermal energy. Each rod has the same length and diameter. A drawing pin is fixed with wax to the far end of each rod, and the other ends are placed in the same flame at the same time. She records the time for each pin to fall.
copper 45 s, aluminium 75 s, brass 120 s, steel 260 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the metals in order from best conductor to worst conductor.
parts.answer: copper, aluminium, brass, steel

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables, other than the length and diameter of the rods, that must be kept the same for a fair test.
parts.answer: Any two: same amount of wax / pin; same distance of pin from the flame; same flame (temperature) and position in it; same starting temperature.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of particles, why metals are good thermal conductors.
parts.answer: Metals have free (delocalised) electrons that gain kinetic energy at the hot end and move quickly through the metal, transferring energy; lattice vibrations also pass energy along.
parts.working: B1 free electrons; B1 they move and carry energy through the metal (plus lattice vibrations).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A crystal of purple potassium manganate(VII) is placed at the bottom of a beaker of water, near one side. That side of the beaker is gently heated. Describe the path of the purple colour.
parts.answer: The purple colour rises above the heated side, moves across the top, sinks on the cooler side and returns along the bottom: a circulating loop.
parts.working: B1 rises above heat; B1 moves across and sinks at the far side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this convection current forms.
parts.answer: Water near the flame is heated and expands; its density decreases so it rises; cooler, denser water sinks to take its place.
parts.working: B1 expands; B1 less dense rises; B1 cooler denser water sinks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cup of hot tea is poured into a wide, shallow saucer to cool it quickly. Explain why the tea cools faster in the saucer.
parts.answer: The exposed surface area is larger, so more energy is lost by evaporation, by convection to the air and by radiation.
parts.working: B1 larger surface area; B1 linked to faster evaporation / radiation / convection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors, other than surface area, that affect the rate at which a surface emits infrared radiation.
parts.answer: The surface temperature; the colour and texture of the surface (dull black emits best).

practice.stem: A solar water heater on a roof in Quetta has a dull black absorbing panel of area 2.0 m², with copper pipes fixed to its front and a layer of foam behind it. On a sunny day the Sun delivers 600 W to each square metre of panel. Only 40 % of this power reaches the 80 kg of water in the tank. Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg °C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the absorbing panel is painted dull black.
parts.answer: Dull black is the best absorber of infrared (and visible) radiation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the copper pipes are fixed to the panel and why the panel is backed with foam.
parts.answer: Copper is a good conductor, so energy passes quickly from the panel to the water; foam is a poor conductor (trapped air), reducing losses from the back.
parts.working: B1 copper good conductor; B1 foam insulates / reduces conduction loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the time needed to heat the water by 20 °C. Give your answer in hours to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The tank is placed above the panel. Explain how the water circulates without a pump.
parts.answer: Water heated in the panel expands, becomes less dense and rises into the tank; colder, denser water from the tank sinks down to the panel – a convection current.
parts.working: B1 heated water less dense and rises; B1 cooler denser water sinks to replace it (convection).

practice.stem: On summer days at Clifton Beach, Karachi, a steady breeze blows in from the Arabian Sea during the afternoon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The specific heat capacity of sand is much lower than that of water. Explain why, on a sunny morning, the land becomes warmer than the sea.
parts.answer: Each kilogram of land needs less energy for each degree rise, so with similar energy received the land's temperature rises faster than the sea's (the sea also mixes the energy through a greater depth).
parts.working: B1 lower specific heat capacity → larger temperature rise for same energy; B1 land heats faster than sea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a breeze blows from the sea towards the land during the afternoon.
parts.answer: Air above the hot land is heated, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises; cooler, denser air from above the sea moves in to replace it; this flow at ground level is the sea breeze (part of a convection current).
parts.working: B1 air over land heated, less dense; B1 warm air rises; B1 cooler air from over the sea flows in to replace it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest and explain the direction of the breeze late at night.
parts.answer: From the land towards the sea: the land cools faster than the sea, so the air above the warmer sea rises and air from the land replaces it.
parts.working: B1 land to sea; B1 sea now warmer than land so convection current is reversed.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Car radiators have many thin metal fins. Explain how the fins increase the rate of energy loss by radiation.
parts.answer: They increase the surface area, and the rate of emission of infrared radiation increases with surface area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An uninsulated hot-water tank loses thermal energy at an average rate of 80 W. Calculate the energy lost in one day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An insulating jacket reduces the rate of loss to 25 W. Calculate the energy saved each day.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert the daily saving into kilowatt-hours. (1 kW h = 3.6 × 10⁶ J)
parts.answer: 1.32 kW h

parts.label: d
parts.text: The jacket is made of foam with a shiny outer surface. Explain how each feature reduces thermal energy loss.
parts.answer: Foam traps air, a poor conductor, and prevents convection; the shiny surface is a poor emitter of infrared radiation.

practice.stem: A hollow metal cube is filled with hot water. Its four vertical faces have different surfaces: dull black, shiny black, dull silver and shiny silver. An infrared detector is placed 10 cm from each face in turn. Readings (arbitrary units): dull black 92, shiny black 78, dull silver 30, shiny silver 12.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two conclusions about how the colour and texture of a surface affect the emission of infrared radiation.
parts.answer: Black surfaces emit more than silver ones; dull (matt) surfaces emit more than shiny ones of the same colour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the detector is placed at the same distance from each face.
parts.answer: The reading depends on distance, so it must be kept constant for a fair comparison.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why all four faces are at the same temperature, and why this matters.
parts.answer: They all touch the same hot water; the rate of emission depends on temperature, so any difference must be due to the surface.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict which surface would warm up fastest if the cube were filled with cold water and placed in sunlight. Explain.
parts.answer: Dull black; good emitters are also good absorbers of infrared radiation.
parts.working: B1 dull black; B1 good emitter = good absorber.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Fish landed at Gwadar are carried to market in boxes of polystyrene foam with crushed ice. Explain why polystyrene foam is used for the boxes.
parts.answer: It contains trapped air, a poor conductor, so little thermal energy conducts in from the warm surroundings; trapped air cannot circulate, so no convection.
parts.working: B1 poor conductor (trapped air); B1 prevents convection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ice is best placed on top of the fish rather than underneath.
parts.answer: Air cooled by the ice becomes denser and sinks over the fish, setting up convection currents that cool the whole box; cold air would stay at the bottom if the ice were underneath.
parts.working: B1 cold air denser, sinks; B1 convection current reaches all fish.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the outside of the boxes is white.
parts.answer: White is a poor absorber of radiation from the Sun.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the nature of (i) an alpha particle, (ii) a beta particle, (iii) gamma radiation.
parts.answer: (i) a helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons) (ii) a high-speed electron (from the nucleus) (iii) an electromagnetic wave

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of the three radiations is (i) the most ionising, (ii) the most penetrating.
parts.answer: (i) alpha (ii) gamma

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is needed to stop most beta particles.
parts.answer: A few millimetres of aluminium

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of radiation is stopped by a single sheet of paper?
A alpha only
B beta only
C gamma only
D beta and gamma
parts.answer: A alpha only
parts.working: Alpha particles are highly ionising and have a very short range; paper absorbs them. Beta (B) needs a few mm of aluminium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by background radiation.
parts.answer: Ionising radiation that is always present in the environment, from natural and artificial sources

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two natural sources and one man-made source of background radiation.
parts.answer: Natural: radon gas from rocks/soil; rocks and building materials; cosmic rays; food and drink. Man-made: medical X-rays / treatments; nuclear power / fallout from weapons tests
parts.working: B1 each, two natural and one man-made

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the background count is higher in some regions than in others.
parts.answer: Different rocks (e.g. granite) contain more radioactive isotopes / more radon; higher altitude has more cosmic rays

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three precautions a technician should take when handling a radioactive source in a school laboratory.
parts.answer: Use long-handled tongs; keep the source pointed away from people; minimise the time it is out; store it in a lead-lined box; wash hands after

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why increasing the distance from a source reduces the risk.
parts.answer: Radiation spreads out and is absorbed by air, so less reaches the person (alpha and beta have short ranges in air)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why ionising radiation is harmful to living cells.
parts.answer: It ionises atoms in cells, damaging molecules such as DNA; this can kill cells or cause mutations / cancer
parts.working: B1 ionisation of molecules in cells; B1 cell death or mutation / cancer

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses a Geiger-Müller tube and counter with no source present. The counter records 30 counts in 2.0 minutes. Calculate the background count rate in counts/min.
parts.answer: 15 counts/min

parts.label: b
parts.text: A source is placed in front of the tube. The count rate is now 465 counts/min. Calculate the count rate due to the source alone.
parts.answer: 450 counts/min

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student measures the background count for several minutes rather than a few seconds.
parts.answer: Decay is random, so a longer count gives a more reliable average

parts.label: a
parts.text: Spent fuel from a nuclear power station contains radioactive isotopes. One of them, caesium-137, has a half-life of 30 years. Calculate how long it takes for its activity to fall to 1/32 of its starting value.
parts.answer: 150 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two precautions taken when storing such waste.
parts.answer: Sealed in thick steel/concrete or glass containers; stored deep underground or in shielded, secure sites away from water supplies; monitored

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage of nuclear power stations compared with gas-fired power stations.
parts.answer: No carbon dioxide emitted while generating / large output from small fuel mass / reliable

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A beam containing alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays passes through a magnetic field. Which radiation is NOT deflected?
A alpha particles
B beta particles
C gamma rays
D none of them; all are deflected
parts.answer: C gamma rays
parts.working: Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves with no charge, so a magnetic field does not deflect them. Alpha and beta particles are charged, so A and B are deflected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by ionisation.
parts.answer: The removal (or addition) of electrons from atoms, so that they become charged ions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Alpha particles travel only a few centimetres in air, but beta particles travel much further. Explain why, in terms of ionisation.
parts.answer: Alpha particles are strongly ionising, so they lose their energy quickly by ionising many air molecules over a short distance; beta particles ionise less, so they keep their energy for longer.
parts.working: B1 alpha highly ionising; B1 loses energy quickly / short range

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which radiation needs several centimetres of lead to reduce it greatly.
parts.answer: Gamma radiation.

practice.stem: A sample contains 2.4 × 10¹² undecayed nuclei of polonium-210. The half-life of polonium-210 is 138 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of half-lives in 414 days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of polonium-210 nuclei that remain undecayed after 414 days.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many nuclei have decayed in this time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the half-life of a radioactive isotope.
parts.answer: The time taken for half the nuclei of the isotope in a sample to decay (or for the activity to halve)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sample has an activity of 1600 Bq. Its half-life is 6 hours. Calculate its activity after 24 hours.
parts.answer: 100 Bq

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how long it takes for the activity to fall to 200 Bq.
parts.answer: 18 hours

parts.label: a
parts.text: Radium-226, ²²⁶₈₈Ra, decays by emitting an alpha particle to form radon (Rn). Write the decay equation, showing the nucleon and proton numbers of the radon nucleus.
parts.answer: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He (or α)
parts.working: B1 alpha as ⁴₂He / ⁴₂α; B1 222; B1 86

parts.label: b
parts.text: Radon is a gas. Explain why breathing in radon is more dangerous than being near a sealed source of radium outside the body.
parts.answer: Alpha particles cannot penetrate skin, but inside the lungs they are emitted next to living cells; they are strongly ionising and damage cells / DNA
parts.working: B1 alpha absorbed by dead skin layer outside body; B1 inside, strong ionisation of nearby cells

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon-14, ¹⁴₆C, decays by beta emission to nitrogen. Write the decay equation.
parts.answer: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e (or β)
parts.working: B1 beta as ⁰₋₁e; B1 nucleon number 14; B1 proton number 7

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the change that takes place inside the nucleus during beta decay.
parts.answer: A neutron changes into a proton and an electron; the electron is emitted at high speed as the beta particle
parts.working: B1 neutron → proton; B1 + electron emitted

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the nucleon number does not change in beta decay.
parts.answer: A neutron is replaced by a proton, so the total number of nucleons stays the same

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A nucleus emits an alpha particle. What happens to its proton number and its nucleon number?
A proton number −2, nucleon number −4
B proton number −4, nucleon number −2
C proton number +1, nucleon number 0
D proton number 0, nucleon number −4
parts.answer: A proton number −2, nucleon number −4
parts.working: An alpha particle contains 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so Z falls by 2 and A falls by 4. C describes beta decay.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Technetium-99m is used as a medical tracer. It emits gamma radiation and has a half-life of 6.0 hours. Explain why a gamma emitter is chosen for a tracer that is injected into a patient.
parts.answer: Gamma passes out of the body so it can be detected outside; it is weakly ionising so causes less damage
parts.working: B1 penetrates tissue to reach the detector; B1 least ionising

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a half-life of a few hours is suitable.
parts.answer: Long enough for the scan to be done; short enough that the activity soon falls, limiting the patient's dose
parts.working: B1 long enough to detect; B1 decays quickly afterwards

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the technetium-99m remaining 24 hours after injection.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about radioactive decay is correct?
A The decay of a nucleus is random and cannot be predicted.
B Heating a sample makes its nuclei decay faster.
C It is possible to predict exactly when a particular nucleus will decay.
D Increasing the pressure on a sample increases its half-life.
parts.answer: A The decay of a nucleus is random and cannot be predicted.
parts.working: Decay is random and spontaneous: it is not affected by temperature or pressure, and we can only predict what fraction of a large sample will decay. B is wrong: half-life is unaffected by physical conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A smoke detector contains a small source of americium-241, an alpha emitter. Alpha particles ionise the air between two plates, so a small current flows. Explain how smoke entering the detector sets off the alarm.
parts.answer: Smoke particles absorb the alpha particles, so less air is ionised; the current falls and the circuit triggers the alarm
parts.working: B1 smoke absorbs alpha / reduces ionisation; B1 current falls, which triggers the alarm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an alpha source is suitable for use in homes.
parts.answer: Alpha is strongly ionising, so a small source gives a measurable current; alpha has a very short range and is stopped by the casing, so it is not a hazard outside the detector
parts.working: B1 strongly ionising; B1 short range / stopped by casing

parts.label: c
parts.text: Americium-241 has a half-life of about 430 years. Explain why this is an advantage.
parts.answer: The activity stays almost constant for the life of the detector, so it does not need replacing

practice.stem:
A Geiger-Müller tube is placed a short distance from a radioactive source. Different absorbers are placed between them. The background count rate is 20 counts/min.
No absorber: 520 counts/min
Thin paper: 515 counts/min
3 mm aluminium: 21 counts/min

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the evidence that the source does not emit alpha particles.
parts.answer: Paper hardly reduces the count rate (520 → 515)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the evidence that the source emits beta particles.
parts.answer: 3 mm of aluminium reduces the count rate greatly, but paper does not (515 → 21)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain whether the source emits gamma radiation.
parts.answer: No: with 3 mm of aluminium the count rate (21 counts/min) is the same as the background (20 counts/min), so no radiation from the source passes through the aluminium
parts.working: B1 no gamma; B1 aluminium reading equals background, but gamma would pass through 3 mm of aluminium almost unabsorbed

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the count rate due to the source when there is no absorber.
parts.answer: 500 counts/min

parts.label: a
parts.text: Uranium-238, ²³⁸₉₂U, decays by alpha emission to thorium (Th). State the nucleon number and proton number of the thorium nucleus.
parts.answer: nucleon number 234; proton number 90

parts.label: b
parts.text: The thorium nucleus then decays by beta emission to protactinium (Pa). State the nucleon number and proton number of the protactinium nucleus.
parts.answer: nucleon number 234; proton number 91

parts.label: c
parts.text: After these two decays, the nucleus sometimes emits gamma radiation. State the effect of gamma emission on the nucleon number and proton number.
parts.answer: No change to either

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The activity of a radioactive sample falls from 960 Bq to 240 Bq in 10 days. What is its half-life?
A 2.5 days
B 5.0 days
C 10 days
D 20 days
parts.answer: B 5.0 days
parts.working: 960 → 480 → 240 is two half-lives in 10 days, so one half-life is 5.0 days. 10 days is the error of treating a fall to a quarter as one half-life.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Strontium-90, ⁹⁰₃₈Sr, decays by beta emission to an isotope of yttrium (Y). Write the nuclear equation.
parts.answer: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e
parts.working: B1 beta particle ⁰₋₁e; B1 nucleon number 90; B1 proton number 39

parts.label: b
parts.text: The yttrium nucleus is left in an excited state and then emits gamma radiation. State the change in its proton number and nucleon number.
parts.answer: No change to either.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Strontium-90 is used to control the thickness of paper in a paper mill. Explain why a beta emitter is chosen.
parts.answer: Beta particles are partly absorbed by paper, so the count rate changes noticeably when the thickness changes; alpha would be stopped completely and gamma would pass straight through.
parts.working: B1 beta partly absorbed by paper; B1 alpha all absorbed / gamma not affected

practice.stem: Radiation from a source passes through a strong electric field between two charged plates, in a vacuum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how alpha and beta particles are deflected compared with each other.
parts.answer: They are deflected in opposite directions; beta particles are deflected much more than alpha particles.
parts.working: B1 opposite directions; B1 beta deflected more

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain each of your observations in (a).
parts.answer: Opposite directions because alpha is positive and beta is negative; beta is deflected more because its mass is much smaller than that of an alpha particle.
parts.working: B1 opposite charges; B1 beta much lighter

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to gamma radiation in the same field, and why.
parts.answer: It is undeflected because it has no charge.

practice.stem: Engineers in Lahore suspect a leak in a water pipe buried 1 m underground. A small amount of a radioactive isotope is added to the water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the isotope must emit gamma radiation.
parts.answer: The radiation has to pass through the soil and the pipe to reach the detector at the surface; alpha and beta would be absorbed.
parts.working: B1 needs to penetrate soil/pipe; B1 alpha/beta absorbed

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable half-life for the isotope. Explain your choice.
parts.answer: A few hours to a few days: long enough to complete the test, short enough that little radioactivity remains in the water supply afterwards.
parts.working: B1 hours–days; B1 reason for both limits

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the leak is found.
parts.answer: A detector is moved along the ground above the pipe; the count rate is highest where the leaking water has collected the isotope in the soil.
parts.working: B1 detector moved along pipe route; B1 high count rate at leak

practice.stem:
A student measures the count rate from a radioactive source with a Geiger-Müller tube and counter. The background count rate is 20 counts/min.
Time / min: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Measured count rate / counts per min: 820, 586, 420, 303, 220, 161

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the background count rate must be subtracted from each reading.
parts.answer: Background radiation is always present, so the measured rate includes counts not from the source

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the corrected count rate at 4.0 min and at 8.0 min.
parts.answer: 400 counts/min; 200 counts/min

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to find the half-life of the source.
parts.answer: 4.0 minutes
parts.working: corrected rate halves from 800 to 400 in 4.0 min (and 400 to 200 in the next 4.0 min) B1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict the count rate the student would measure at 12 minutes.
parts.answer: 120 counts/min
parts.working: corrected = 800 ÷ 8 = 100 (3 half-lives) M1; measured = 100 + 20 = 120 counts/min A1

parts.label: e
parts.text: Explain why the readings do not follow a perfectly smooth curve when repeated.
parts.answer: Radioactive decay is random (counts fluctuate)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A factory makes thin aluminium foil. A radioactive source is placed on one side of the foil and a detector on the other, to monitor the thickness. State which type of radiation should be used. Explain why the other two types are unsuitable.
parts.answer: Beta
parts.working: B1 beta; B1 alpha would be completely stopped by the foil whatever its thickness; B1 gamma would pass through almost unchanged, so small thickness changes would not affect the count

parts.label: b
parts.text: The count rate at the detector suddenly increases. State what has happened to the foil and what the control system should do.
parts.answer: The foil has become thinner; the rollers should be moved apart (less pressure)
parts.working: B1 thinner; B1 adjust rollers to increase thickness

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest whether the source should have a long or short half-life. Explain.
parts.answer: Long, so that the count rate does not fall noticeably during use (and the source need not be replaced often)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Living wood contains carbon-14, which has a half-life of 5700 years. When a tree dies, the carbon-14 in it decays and is not replaced. A wooden bowl found at an archaeological site has a carbon-14 activity that is 1/8 of the activity of the same mass of living wood. Calculate the age of the bowl.
parts.answer: 17100 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another sample has 25 % of the activity of living wood. Calculate its age.
parts.answer: 11400 years

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why carbon dating cannot be used for an object thought to be about 100 years old.
parts.answer: Very little of the carbon-14 has decayed in 100 years (much less than one half-life); the change in activity is too small to measure accurately against random fluctuations
parts.working: B1 100 years is tiny compared with the half-life; B1 activity change too small to detect

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital receives 80 mg of iodine-131, which has a half-life of 8 days. Calculate the mass of iodine-131 remaining after 40 days.
parts.answer: 2.5 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of iodine-131 that has decayed in this time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The iodine-131 emits beta particles. State one reason why used waste from the hospital must be stored safely before disposal.
parts.answer: It is still radioactive and its emissions can ionise and damage living cells; it must be stored until the activity is very low

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the smallest whole number of half-lives after which the mass of iodine-131 is less than 1.0 mg, and state this time in days.
parts.answer: 56 days
parts.working: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 → 5 → 2.5 → 1.25 → 0.625 mg: first below 1.0 mg after 7 half-lives M1; 7 × 8 = 56 days A1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Gamma radiation is used to sterilise sealed packs of surgical instruments. Explain why gamma radiation is used rather than alpha or beta.
parts.answer: Gamma penetrates the sealed packaging to reach the instruments; alpha and beta would be absorbed by the packaging
parts.working: B1 gamma penetrates packaging; B1 alpha/beta absorbed

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the radiation sterilises the instruments.
parts.answer: It kills bacteria / microorganisms by damaging their cells (ionisation)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the instruments do not become radioactive.
parts.answer: Gamma rays do not change the nuclei of the atoms in the instruments; the instruments are irradiated, not contaminated (no radioactive material is left on them)
parts.working: B1 nuclei unchanged; B1 difference between irradiation and contamination

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the source used has a long half-life.
parts.answer: So the activity remains roughly constant and the source does not need frequent replacement

practice.stem: A radioactive isotope X decays into a stable isotope Y with a half-life of 1.3 × 10⁹ years. A rock sample contains 1 atom of X for every 7 atoms of Y.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fraction of the original isotope X that remains in the rock.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of half-lives that have passed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the age of the rock.
parts.answer: 3.9 × 10⁹ years

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one assumption made in this calculation.
parts.answer: There was no Y in the rock when it formed / no X or Y has escaped from the rock.

practice.stem: A sample contains two radioactive isotopes. At the start each has an activity of 1600 Bq. Isotope A has a half-life of 2.0 hours and isotope B has a half-life of 6.0 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the activity of each isotope after 12 hours.
parts.answer: A: 25 Bq; B: 400 Bq
parts.working: M1 A: 6 half-lives; B: 2 half-lives; A1 1600 ÷ 64 = 25 Bq; A1 1600 ÷ 4 = 400 Bq

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total activity after 12 hours.
parts.answer: 425 Bq

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the overall shape of a graph of total activity against time would show that two isotopes are present.
parts.answer: The activity first falls quickly (A decaying), then falls much more slowly with a half-life of 6 h once A has mostly gone; the curve is not a single steady halving.
parts.working: B1 fast initial fall; B1 slower later fall with longer half-life

practice.stem:
The table describes four radioactive isotopes.
Isotope P: emits alpha; half-life 430 years
Isotope Q: emits beta; half-life 29 years
Isotope R: emits gamma; half-life 6 hours
Isotope S: emits gamma; half-life 5.3 years

parts.label: a
parts.text: Choose the most suitable isotope for each use and give a reason in each case: (i) smoke detector, (ii) monitoring the thickness of cardboard, (iii) medical tracer injected into a patient, (iv) sterilising sealed medical equipment.
parts.answer: (i) P: alpha ionises air strongly but is stopped easily, long half-life so it lasts for years. (ii) Q: beta is partly absorbed by cardboard, long half-life gives steady count. (iii) R: gamma escapes the body to be detected, short half-life limits the dose. (iv) S: gamma penetrates the sealed packaging, half-life of years gives a steady supply.
parts.working: B1 each correct choice; B1 each valid reason (radiation type or half-life)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sodium nucleus is represented as ²³₁₁Na. State the proton number and the nucleon number of this nuclide.
parts.answer: proton number 11; nucleon number 23

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of neutrons in the nucleus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of electrons in a neutral atom of sodium-23. Explain your answer.
parts.working: B1 11; B1 a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two nuclides are isotopes of the same element. What must they have the same number of?
A nucleons
B neutrons
C protons
D particles in the nucleus
parts.answer: C protons
parts.working: Isotopes have the same proton number but different numbers of neutrons, so their nucleon numbers differ. B is the reverse of the definition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Copy and complete the information for the three particles in an atom, giving the relative charge and relative mass of each: proton, neutron, electron.
parts.answer: proton: +1, mass 1; neutron: 0, mass 1; electron: −1, mass about 1/1840 (negligible)
parts.working: B1 each particle with both values correct

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in the atom each particle is found.
parts.answer: Protons and neutrons in the nucleus; electrons orbit outside the nucleus

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an atom has no overall charge.
parts.answer: It has equal numbers of protons and electrons, whose charges are equal and opposite

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A neutral atom loses one electron. What does it become?
A a positive ion
B a negative ion
C an atom of a different element
D an isotope of the same element
parts.answer: A a positive ion
parts.working: With one more proton than electrons the particle has an overall positive charge. C is wrong: the element depends only on the proton number, which is unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The nuclide of iron is ⁵⁶₂₆Fe. What does its nucleus contain?
A 26 protons and 30 neutrons
B 26 protons and 56 neutrons
C 30 protons and 26 neutrons
D 56 protons and 26 neutrons
parts.answer: A 26 protons and 30 neutrons
parts.working: Proton number = 26; neutrons = 56 − 26 = 30. B treats the nucleon number as the number of neutrons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A nucleus contains 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Write its nuclide notation, using C as the symbol.
parts.answer: ¹⁴₆C
parts.working: B1 nucleon number 14; B1 proton number 6

parts.label: b
parts.text: A nucleus of lithium contains 3 protons and has a nucleon number of 7. State the number of neutrons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of electrons in a neutral lithium atom.
parts.working: B1 equal to the number of protons

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the number of neutrons for each nuclide: oxygen ¹⁶₈O, iron ⁵⁶₂₆Fe and gold ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au.
parts.answer: oxygen 8; iron 30; gold 118

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of these nuclei has the largest positive charge.
parts.answer: Gold (79 protons).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the nuclear model of the atom.
parts.answer: A very small, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre containing protons and neutrons; electrons orbit the nucleus; most of the atom is empty space.
parts.working: B1 small dense positive nucleus; B1 protons and neutrons in nucleus; B1 electrons orbit / mostly empty space

parts.label: b
parts.text: The diameter of an atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ m and the diameter of its nucleus is about 10⁻¹⁵ m. Calculate how many times larger the atom is than the nucleus.
parts.answer: about 100 000 (10⁵) times

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the earlier 'plum pudding' model of the atom.
parts.answer: A sphere of positive charge spread throughout, with negative electrons embedded in it.
parts.working: B1 positive charge spread out; B1 electrons embedded

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which the nuclear model differs from the plum pudding model.
parts.answer: The positive charge (and almost all the mass) is concentrated in a tiny nucleus; most of the atom is empty space; electrons are outside the nucleus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An oxygen atom ¹⁶₈O gains two electrons to form an oxide ion, O²⁻. State the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion.
parts.answer: 8 protons, 8 neutrons, 10 electrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the ion has a negative charge.
parts.answer: It has more electrons (10) than protons (8).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define proton number and nucleon number.
parts.answer: Proton number: the number of protons in the nucleus. Nucleon number: the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sulfur nucleus is ³²₁₆S. Calculate the number of neutrons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: One neutron is added to this nucleus. State whether it is still sulfur and write its new nuclide notation.
parts.answer: Yes, still sulfur (same proton number); ³³₁₆S

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an experiment, a beam of alpha particles is directed at a very thin sheet of gold foil in a vacuum. Describe what is observed about the paths of the alpha particles.
parts.answer: Most pass straight through undeflected; a few are deflected through small angles; a very small number are deflected through large angles (some bounce back)
parts.working: B1 most go straight through; B1 some deflected; B1 very few deflected through more than 90°

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what each observation shows about the structure of the atom.
parts.answer: Most of the atom is empty space; the nucleus is positively charged (repels the positive alpha particles); the nucleus is very small and contains most of the mass (large deflections are rare)
parts.working: B1 mostly empty space; B1 nucleus positive; B1 nucleus tiny and dense / contains most of the mass

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the experiment is carried out in a vacuum.
parts.answer: Alpha particles have a very short range in air; air molecules would absorb / deflect them

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many neutrons are in a nucleus of ²³⁵₉₂U?
A 92
B 143
C 235
D 327
parts.working: Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number = 235 − 92 = 143. D adds the two numbers instead of subtracting.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a fusion reactor two isotopes of hydrogen join:
²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + X
Use the conservation of nucleon number and proton number to identify particle X.
parts.answer: X is a neutron, ¹₀n
parts.working: nucleon number 2 + 3 − 4 = 1, proton number 1 + 1 − 2 = 0 M1; neutron A1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why fusion only happens at extremely high temperatures, such as in the core of the Sun.
parts.answer: Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other; they need very high kinetic energy (speed) to get close enough to fuse
parts.working: B1 electrostatic repulsion between positive nuclei; B1 high temperature gives high enough kinetic energy

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one difference between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
parts.answer: Fission splits a large nucleus into smaller ones; fusion joins small nuclei to form a larger one

parts.label: a
parts.text: Carbon-14 is ¹⁴₆C and nitrogen-14 is ¹⁴₇N. Calculate the number of neutrons in each nucleus.
parts.answer: carbon-14: 8; nitrogen-14: 7

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says these are isotopes because they have the same nucleon number. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Isotopes must have the same proton number (same element); these have different proton numbers (6 and 7), so they are different elements
parts.working: B1 isotopes need same proton number; B1 these have 6 and 7 protons

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which of the two nuclei has the greater positive charge. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Nitrogen-14, because it has 7 protons and carbon-14 has only 6
parts.working: B1 nitrogen-14 with reason: more protons (7 v 6); neutrons carry no charge

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of nuclides are isotopes of the same element?
A ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N
B ¹⁶₈O and ¹⁸₈O
C ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca
D ²³₁₁Na and ²⁴₁₂Mg
parts.answer: B ¹⁶₈O and ¹⁸₈O
parts.working: Isotopes have the same proton number but different numbers of neutrons: both oxygen nuclides have 8 protons. A and C have the same nucleon number but different proton numbers, so they are different elements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hydrogen has three isotopes: hydrogen-1, hydrogen-2 (deuterium) and hydrogen-3 (tritium). State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why all three isotopes behave in the same way in chemical reactions.
parts.answer: They have the same number of electrons (chemistry depends on electrons).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which water made with deuterium ('heavy water') differs physically from ordinary water.
parts.answer: It has a greater density (its molecules are more massive).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an alpha-scattering experiment, very thin gold foil is used. Explain why a very small fraction of alpha particles bounce back towards the source.
parts.answer: They come very close to a nucleus, which is small, massive and positive; the strong repulsion turns them back.
parts.working: B1 near-head-on approach to nucleus; B1 large repulsive force from concentrated positive charge (massive nucleus)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the results would change if the foil were made of aluminium (proton number 13) instead of gold (proton number 79), with the same thickness.
parts.answer: Fewer large-angle deflections, because each aluminium nucleus has a much smaller positive charge so the repulsion is weaker.
parts.working: B1 fewer/smaller large deflections; B1 smaller nuclear charge

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the foil must be very thin.
parts.answer: So that each alpha particle is scattered by only one nucleus (and is not absorbed).

practice.stem:
In a reactor, one possible fission of uranium-235 is:
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁰₅₄Xe + ⁹⁴₃₈Sr + x ¹₀n

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of x.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the proton numbers are balanced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the neutrons released in the reactor.
parts.answer: Some cause further fissions of uranium-235 nuclei (a chain reaction); others are absorbed by control rods.
parts.working: B1 cause more fissions; B1 absorbed by control rods / escape

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two deuterium nuclei fuse: ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₂He + X. Identify X.
parts.answer: A neutron, ¹₀n
parts.working: M1 nucleon number 4 − 3 = 1 and proton number 2 − 2 = 0; A1 neutron

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why fusion needs a very high temperature.
parts.answer: Both nuclei are positive and repel; they must move extremely fast (high kinetic energy) to get close enough to fuse.
parts.working: B1 repulsion between positive nuclei; B1 very high speed/energy needed

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where fusion happens naturally.
parts.answer: In the cores of stars such as the Sun.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the energy changes in a nuclear power station, from the fuel to the electrical output.
parts.answer: Nuclear energy released by fission → thermal energy in the reactor core → heats water to make steam → kinetic energy of turbine → electrical energy from the generator.
parts.working: B1 nuclear to thermal; B1 steam drives turbine (kinetic); B1 generator produces electrical

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage of nuclear power compared with solar power.
parts.answer: Radioactive waste must be stored safely for a very long time / risk of accidents.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what an alpha particle is made of and give its symbol.
parts.answer: 2 protons and 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus), ⁴₂He

parts.label: b
parts.text: Alpha particles emitted by uranium in underground rock gradually slow down and stop. Explain how they become helium atoms.
parts.answer: Each alpha particle has a charge of +2; when it stops it picks up two electrons from its surroundings, becoming a neutral helium atom.
parts.working: B1 charge +2; B1 gains two electrons

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why helium gas is found trapped in some natural-gas deposits.
parts.answer: It has been produced over millions of years by alpha decay in surrounding rocks and trapped underground.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a nuclear reactor a nucleus of uranium-235 absorbs a neutron and splits:
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n
Calculate x, the number of neutrons released.
parts.working: nucleon numbers: 235 + 1 = 141 + 92 + x M1; x = 3 A1 (proton numbers: 92 = 56 + 36 ✓)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of this process.
parts.answer: Nuclear fission

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this reaction can lead to a chain reaction, and how the chain reaction is controlled in a reactor.
parts.answer: The neutrons released can be absorbed by other U-235 nuclei, causing more fissions, each releasing more neutrons; control rods (e.g. boron) absorb some neutrons so that on average only one neutron from each fission causes a further fission
parts.working: B1 released neutrons cause further fissions; B1 control rods absorb neutrons; B1 so the rate stays steady

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the form in which most of the energy released first appears.
parts.answer: Kinetic energy of the fission products (daughter nuclei and neutrons)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Chlorine has two common isotopes, ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl. State the numbers of protons and neutrons in each.
parts.answer: Cl-35: 17 protons, 18 neutrons; Cl-37: 17 protons, 20 neutrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why both isotopes have the same chemical properties.
parts.answer: They have the same number of protons, so the same number of electrons in the neutral atom; chemical behaviour depends on the electrons
parts.working: B1 same proton number / electrons; B1 chemistry depends on electrons

parts.label: c
parts.text: A chloride ion, Cl⁻, is formed from a chlorine-37 atom. State the number of electrons in the ion.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the two isotopes have different masses even though they are the same element.
parts.answer: Cl-37 has two more neutrons, and neutrons have mass

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total charge of the nucleus of an oxygen-16 atom, ¹⁶₈O. (Charge of a proton = +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the total charge of all the electrons in a neutral oxygen atom.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the neutrons do not affect the charge of the nucleus but do affect its mass.
parts.answer: Neutrons have zero charge but a mass about equal to that of a proton (relative mass 1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In 1919 nitrogen was bombarded with alpha particles: ¹⁴₇N + ⁴₂He → ¹⁷₈O + X. Identify X.
parts.answer: A proton, ¹₁H (¹₁p)
parts.working: M1 nucleon number 18 − 17 = 1, proton number 9 − 8 = 1; A1 proton

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aluminium bombarded with alpha particles: ²⁷₁₃Al + ⁴₂He → ³⁰₁₅P + Y. Identify Y.
parts.answer: A neutron, ¹₀n
parts.working: M1 nucleon number 31 − 30 = 1, proton number 15 − 15 = 0; A1 neutron

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the quantities that are conserved in every nuclear reaction, as shown by these equations.
parts.answer: Nucleon number (mass number) and proton number (charge).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The diameter of an atom is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and that of its nucleus is about 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. A model is made in which the nucleus is a marble 1.0 cm across. Calculate the diameter of the atom in the model.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Almost all the mass of the atom is in the nucleus. Use the model to explain why the density of nuclear matter is enormous.
parts.answer: The atom's mass is packed into a volume about 10¹² times smaller than the atom (ratio of diameters cubed), so the density is huge.
parts.working: B1 mass concentrated in nucleus; B1 volume ratio 10¹² / tiny volume

parts.label: a
parts.text: A neutral atom has a nucleon number of 40, and its nucleus has 4 more neutrons than protons. Calculate the numbers of protons and neutrons.
parts.answer: 18 protons, 22 neutrons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Element 18 is argon (Ar). Write the nuclide notation.
parts.answer: ⁴⁰₁₈Ar

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calcium-40 has 20 protons. Explain why argon-40 and calcium-40 are not isotopes.
parts.answer: Isotopes must have the same proton number; these have different proton numbers (18 and 20), so they are different elements, even though the nucleon number is the same.
parts.working: B1 different proton numbers; B1 so different elements

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why neutrons, rather than protons, are used to cause fission in uranium-235.
parts.answer: Neutrons have no charge, so they are not repelled by the positive nucleus and can enter it even at low speed; protons would be repelled.
parts.working: B1 neutron uncharged; B1 protons repelled by positive nucleus

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the same idea to explain why fusion is much harder to start than fission.
parts.answer: In fusion two positive nuclei must be forced together against their repulsion, needing extreme temperatures; fission only needs an uncharged neutron to be absorbed.
parts.working: B1 fusion needs two positive nuclei to approach (repulsion); B1 so very high temperature needed

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one advantage fusion would have over fission as an energy source.
parts.answer: Fuel (hydrogen isotopes) is plentiful / far less long-lived radioactive waste.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In one reactor design each fission releases neutrons, but on average exactly one neutron from each fission causes another fission. Describe what happens to the rate of fission.
parts.answer: It stays constant (steady chain reaction).

parts.label: b
parts.text: If control rods were removed so that on average 2 neutrons from each fission caused further fissions, calculate the number of fissions in the 10th generation that start from one fission in the 1st generation.
parts.working: M1 number doubles each generation: 2^(n − 1); A1 2⁹ = 512

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how control rods keep the chain reaction steady.
parts.answer: Control rods absorb neutrons; lowering them further in absorbs more neutrons so fewer fissions occur; raising them allows more.
parts.working: B1 absorb neutrons; B1 depth adjusted to keep one fission per fission

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is a light-year?
A the time light takes to reach the Earth from the Sun
B the distance travelled by light in a vacuum in one year
C the time for the Earth to orbit the Sun
D the brightness of a star seen from one year away
parts.answer: B the distance travelled by light in a vacuum in one year
parts.working: A light-year is a unit of distance: the distance light travels through a vacuum in one year (about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m). A confuses it with a time.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which two elements make up most of the Sun?
A hydrogen and helium
B hydrogen and oxygen
C helium and carbon
D iron and nickel
parts.answer: A hydrogen and helium
parts.working: The Sun is mostly hydrogen with helium (made by fusion). Iron and nickel make up much of the Earth's core, not the Sun.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Sun is described as a medium-sized star. State the source of its energy.
parts.answer: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium in its core.
parts.working: B1 nuclear fusion; B1 hydrogen → helium.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the three regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in which the Sun emits most of its energy.
parts.answer: Infrared, visible light and ultraviolet.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why the Sun appears much brighter than other stars.
parts.answer: It is much closer to the Earth than any other star.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a galaxy.
parts.answer: A very large group of (billions of) stars held together by gravity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the galaxy that contains the Solar System.
parts.answer: The Milky Way

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that one light-year is about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m. Take one year as 365.25 days and the speed of light as 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The diameter of the Milky Way is about 100 000 light-years. State what this tells you about the time light takes to cross it.
parts.answer: Light takes about 100 000 years to cross it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these stages in the life cycle of a star like the Sun in the correct order: red giant, interstellar cloud of dust and gas, white dwarf, protostar, stable star, planetary nebula.
parts.answer: Interstellar cloud → protostar → stable star → red giant → planetary nebula (with a white dwarf left at the centre).
parts.working: B3 fully correct; B2 one stage misplaced; B1 first two correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the main element present in the cloud from which a star forms.
parts.answer: Hydrogen

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the force that pulls the cloud together to form a protostar.
parts.answer: Gravity (gravitational attraction)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which list puts these stars in order of surface temperature, from coolest to hottest?
A red, yellow, blue-white
B blue-white, yellow, red
C yellow, red, blue-white
D red, blue-white, yellow
parts.answer: A red, yellow, blue-white
parts.working: The colour of a star shows its surface temperature: red stars are the coolest, yellow stars (like the Sun) are hotter, and blue-white stars are the hottest. B reverses the order; C and D put a red or yellow star in the wrong place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A star like the Sun releases energy in its core. State what happens to the hydrogen nuclei in the core and name the nucleus that is formed.
parts.answer: The hydrogen nuclei fuse (join) together to form helium nuclei, releasing energy.
parts.working: B1 hydrogen nuclei join / fuse together; B1 helium nuclei formed (energy released).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the star does not collapse under its own gravity while it is in its stable stage.
parts.answer: The energy released produces an outward pressure (radiation pressure) which balances the inward pull of gravity.
parts.working: B1 energy release gives an outward force / pressure; B1 this balances the inward gravitational force, so the star is stable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says that Venus is a star. Explain why this is incorrect.
parts.answer: Venus is a planet: it does not give out its own light but reflects light from the Sun. A star gives out its own light and energy from fusion in its core.
parts.working: B1 Venus reflects sunlight (it does not produce its own light); B1 stars produce their own light and energy by nuclear fusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other planet of the Solar System that can be seen with the naked eye.
parts.answer: Mars, Jupiter or Saturn (any one of these)
parts.working: B1 any one of Mars, Jupiter, Saturn (Mercury is also acceptable).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A star is 550 light-years from the Earth. One light-year is 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. Calculate the distance to the star in metres. Give your answer in standard form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how long ago the light we now see from the star left it.
parts.answer: 550 years ago
parts.working: B1 550 years (the light takes 550 years to travel that distance).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the star may look different now from the way it looked when this light left it.
parts.answer: The star may have changed (for example it may have aged or even exploded) during the 550 years, so we see its past appearance.
parts.working: B1 the star has had 550 years to change; we see the past.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these objects in order of size, from smallest to largest: Milky Way galaxy, Moon, Solar System, Universe, Earth.
parts.answer: Moon, Earth, Solar System, Milky Way galaxy, Universe
parts.working: B1 Moon smallest, then Earth; B1 Solar System, then the Milky Way, then the Universe in the correct order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the force that keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth.
parts.answer: Gravity (the gravitational force of the Earth)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A star with a mass about twenty times that of the Sun reaches the end of its stable life. Which sequence is correct?
A red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
B red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
C white dwarf → red giant → supernova
D protostar → red supergiant → white dwarf
parts.answer: B red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
parts.working: Very massive stars expand into red supergiants and explode as supernovae, leaving a neutron star or (for the most massive) a black hole. A is the path for a star like the Sun.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A stable star stays the same size for billions of years. Explain why, in terms of the forces acting.
parts.answer: The inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward force (pressure) due to the high temperature from fusion in the core.
parts.working: B1 gravity pulls inwards; B1 balanced by outward pressure from fusion energy / high temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to a star like the Sun when most of the hydrogen in its core has been used.
parts.answer: Fusion in the core slows; the outer layers expand and cool, forming a red giant.
parts.working: B1 expands; B1 becomes a red giant (outer layers cooler, red).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what remains at the end of the life of a star like the Sun.
parts.answer: The outer layers drift away as a planetary nebula, leaving a small hot dense core called a white dwarf.
parts.working: B1 planetary nebula; B1 white dwarf.

practice.stem: Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to the Sun, at a distance of 4.2 light-years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance to Proxima Centauri in metres. One light-year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how long ago the light now reaching us from Proxima Centauri left the star.
parts.answer: 4.2 years ago

parts.label: c
parts.text: A newspaper says a star 'might no longer exist even though we can see it'. Explain how this can be true for a very distant star.
parts.answer: Light from a star thousands or millions of light-years away left it that many years ago; the star may have ended its life since then, but its old light is still arriving.
parts.working: B1 light takes a long time (years = distance in ly) to reach us; B1 we see the star as it was, it may have changed/died since.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by redshift.
parts.answer: An increase in the observed wavelength of electromagnetic radiation (e.g. light) from stars and galaxies that are moving away from us.
parts.working: B1 increase in observed wavelength (shift towards red end); B1 because the source is receding / moving away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Light from almost all distant galaxies shows redshift. State two conclusions about the Universe.
parts.answer: Galaxies are moving away from us; the Universe is expanding (more distant galaxies move away faster).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how redshift supports the Big Bang theory.
parts.answer: If galaxies are moving apart now, they were closer together in the past – the Universe began from a single very small, very hot region.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name one other piece of evidence for the Big Bang theory.
parts.answer: Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR).

practice.stem: New stars are forming in the Orion Nebula, a huge cloud of dust and gas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a protostar forms from an interstellar cloud.
parts.answer: Gravity pulls the dust and gas together; the cloud collapses into a dense, hot ball (protostar).
parts.working: B1 gravitational attraction pulls particles together; B1 cloud contracts into a dense clump.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the protostar becomes hotter as it contracts.
parts.answer: Gravitational potential energy of the falling material is converted into kinetic energy of the particles, so the temperature rises.
parts.working: B1 loss of gravitational potential energy; B1 converted to kinetic energy (thermal energy) of particles.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what must happen in the protostar for it to become a stable star.
parts.answer: Its core must become hot enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse into helium.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Some interstellar clouds contain elements such as iron and carbon as well as hydrogen. Suggest where these heavier elements came from.
parts.answer: They were made by fusion in earlier stars and scattered by supernovae (and planetary nebulae).

practice.stem:
An astronomy club in Karachi studies four stable stars:
star P: 0.8 times the mass of the Sun
star Q: 1.0 times the mass of the Sun
star R: 12 times the mass of the Sun
star S: 30 times the mass of the Sun

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which stars will end as white dwarfs.
parts.answer: P and Q

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the stage that star R reaches after it leaves the stable stage.
parts.answer: Red supergiant

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify which star is most likely to end as a black hole and give a reason.
parts.answer: S – it is the most massive; after a supernova the most massive remnants collapse into black holes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe what remains after star R explodes as a supernova.
parts.answer: A neutron star at the centre, surrounded by a nebula of gas and dust containing heavier elements.
parts.working: B1 neutron star; B1 nebula (containing heavier elements) spreads out.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the Milky Way is correct?
A It is a single very large star.
B It is a spiral galaxy of billions of stars, and the Solar System lies in one of its spiral arms.
C It is an elliptical galaxy with no gas or dust.
D It is the largest object in the Universe.
parts.answer: B It is a spiral galaxy of billions of stars, and the Solar System lies in one of its spiral arms.
parts.working: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy containing billions of stars; the Solar System is in one of its spiral arms. A is wrong because it is a galaxy, not a star. C describes an elliptical galaxy and the Milky Way is a spiral. D is wrong because the Universe contains many galaxies larger than the Milky Way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Sun becomes a red giant when the hydrogen in its core runs out.
parts.answer: The core contracts and heats up; the outer layers expand and cool, so the star's surface looks red.
parts.working: B1 core contracts and gets hotter; B1 outer layers expand and cool (surface appears red).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the stage that follows the red giant stage and describe what happens to the outer layers of the star.
parts.answer: A planetary nebula; the outer layers are thrown off into space as a shell of gas.
parts.working: B1 planetary nebula; B1 outer layers ejected into space as gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name of the star's final stage and compare its size with the Earth.
parts.answer: A white dwarf, which is about the size of the Earth.
parts.working: B1 white dwarf; B1 about Earth-sized (and very dense).

practice.stem:
Astronomers measure the speed at which four distant galaxies move away from the Earth:
galaxy 1: distance 2.0 × 10²⁴ m, speed 4.4 × 10⁶ m/s
galaxy 2: distance 3.5 × 10²⁴ m, speed 7.7 × 10⁶ m/s
galaxy 3: distance 5.0 × 10²⁴ m, speed 1.1 × 10⁷ m/s
galaxy 4: distance 8.0 × 10²⁴ m, speed 1.76 × 10⁷ m/s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the value of v ÷ d for each galaxy and state its unit. Give each value to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second (s⁻¹) for every galaxy
parts.working: M1 v ÷ d for each galaxy (4.4 × 10⁶ ÷ 2.0 × 10²⁴ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ etc.); A1 all 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what these results show about the relationship between the distance of a galaxy and its speed of recession.
parts.answer: The further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from the Earth (speed is proportional to distance).
parts.working: B1 greater distance gives greater recession speed; the ratio is constant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the value of v ÷ d from part (a) to predict the speed at which a galaxy 1.2 × 10²⁵ m from the Earth is moving away.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Star A and star B look equally bright when viewed from the Earth. Star A is twice as far from the Earth as star B. Explain which star gives out more energy each second.
parts.answer: Star A gives out more energy each second. It is further away, so less of its light reaches the Earth; to look equally bright it must emit more energy.
parts.working: B1 star A must emit more energy per second; B1 further away, so the light is spread over a larger area and less reaches the Earth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the apparent brightness of a star.
parts.answer: The brightness of a star as seen from the Earth, which depends on both its energy output and its distance from the Earth.
parts.working: B1 brightness as seen from Earth (depends on output and distance).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A white dwarf has a mass of 2.0 × 10³⁰ kg and is approximately a sphere of radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m. Calculate its volume in m³, using V = 4/3 × π × r³. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average density of the white dwarf in kg/m³ to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.4 × 10⁹ kg/m³
parts.working: M1 density = mass ÷ volume = 2.0 × 10³⁰ ÷ 1.44 × 10²¹; A1 1.4 × 10⁹ kg/m³.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Water has a density of 1.0 × 10³ kg/m³. State how many times denser than water the white dwarf is.
parts.answer: About 1.4 × 10⁶ times (about 1.4 million times)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The Hubble constant is 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second. A galaxy is 1.0 × 10²⁴ m from the Earth. What is the speed at which it is moving away from the Earth?
A 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s
B 4.5 × 10⁴¹ m/s
C 4.5 × 10⁻⁷ m/s
D 2.2 × 10⁻⁴² m/s
parts.working: v = H₀d = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 1.0 × 10²⁴ = 2.2 × 10⁶ m/s. B comes from dividing d by H₀ instead of multiplying (that gives a time-like quantity, not a speed).

practice.stem: Astronomers measure the redshift of a distant galaxy and find it is moving away from the Earth at 1.5 × 10⁷ m/s. The Hubble constant H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance to the galaxy in metres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert this distance into light-years. One light-year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m.
parts.answer: 7.2 × 10⁸ light-years

parts.label: c
parts.text: The quantity 1/H₀ gives an estimate of the age of the Universe. Calculate this age in years.
parts.answer: 4.5 × 10¹⁷ s ≈ 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years (about 14 billion years)
parts.working: C1 1 ÷ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ = 4.5 × 10¹⁷ s; C1 one year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s; A1 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how astronomers can find the distance to a far galaxy without using its speed.
parts.answer: By measuring the brightness of a supernova in it (supernovae of a particular type have a known brightness, so the dimmer it looks the further away it is).

practice.stem: Galaxy A is 3.0 × 10²⁴ m from the Earth and galaxy B is 1.2 × 10²⁵ m from the Earth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the speed at which each galaxy is moving away from the Earth. H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second.
parts.working: C1 v = H₀d; A1 both: 6.6 × 10⁶ m/s and 2.64 × 10⁷ m/s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which galaxy shows the greater redshift. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Galaxy B – it is moving away faster, and a greater recession speed produces a greater increase in observed wavelength.
parts.working: B1 B; B1 greater speed of recession → greater redshift.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says: 'All galaxies are moving away from the Earth, so the Earth must be at the centre of the Universe.' Explain why this conclusion is not correct.
parts.answer: Space itself is expanding, so an observer in any galaxy would see all other galaxies moving away from them; there is no centre.
parts.working: B1 the Universe/space is expanding uniformly; B1 observers anywhere see the same – no special centre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens in the core of a very massive star near the end of its life, leading to a supernova.
parts.answer: Fusion makes heavier and heavier elements up to iron; when fusion can no longer release energy, the core collapses under gravity and the outer layers are blown off in a huge explosion (supernova).
parts.working: B1 heavier elements formed by fusion (up to iron) in a red supergiant; B1 core collapses / star explodes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why scientists say 'the iron in your blood was made inside stars'.
parts.answer: Elements heavier than helium (such as iron) are made by fusion inside stars and released by supernovae into nebulae; the Solar System formed from such a nebula, so its material includes these elements.
parts.working: B1 heavy elements made in stars / supernovae; B1 scattered into a nebula from which the Sun, Earth (and we) formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Sun will not become a supernova.
parts.answer: Its mass is too small; it will become a red giant then a white dwarf.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why a black hole cannot be seen directly.
parts.answer: Its gravitational field is so strong that not even light can escape from it.

practice.stem: In the 1960s, radio engineers found a faint signal that their antenna picked up whichever direction it pointed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR).
parts.answer: Microwave radiation of a particular frequency that is detected coming from all directions in space (very evenly).
parts.working: B1 microwave radiation; B1 coming from all directions / everywhere in space.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the CMBR was produced and why it is now detected as microwaves.
parts.answer: It was emitted shortly after the Universe formed, when the Universe was very hot (short-wavelength radiation); as the Universe expanded, the wavelength of the radiation was stretched (increased) so it is now in the microwave region.
parts.working: B1 produced shortly after the Universe began / when the Universe was very hot; B1 Universe has expanded since; B1 wavelength stretched / increased into the microwave region.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the CMBR supports the Big Bang theory.
parts.answer: It is the leftover radiation predicted from a hot, dense early Universe that has since expanded and cooled.

practice.stem: Light from a distant galaxy takes 9.0 × 10⁸ years to reach the Earth. H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the distance to the galaxy in metres. One light-year is 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. Give your answer in standard form to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use Hubble's law, v = H₀ × d, to calculate the speed at which the galaxy is moving away from the Earth. H₀ = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ per second. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why astronomers say that the light from the galaxy shows the galaxy as it was 9.0 × 10⁸ years ago.
parts.answer: Light takes time to travel through space, so the light that arrives today left the galaxy 900 million years ago; we see the galaxy as it was then.
parts.working: B1 light takes 9.0 × 10⁸ years to reach the Earth; B1 so the image shows the galaxy's past, not its present appearance.

practice.stem: The Sun is about 2.6 × 10²⁰ m from the centre of the Milky Way. It takes about 2.3 × 10⁸ years to complete one orbit of the centre. Take one year as 3.16 × 10⁷ s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time, in seconds, for the Sun to complete one orbit of the centre of the Milky Way. Give your answer in standard form to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use v = 2πr ÷ T to calculate the average orbital speed of the Sun in m/s. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Sun moves in a circle around the centre of the galaxy instead of moving off in a straight line.
parts.answer: The gravitational pull of the galaxy's mass acts towards its centre; this resultant force keeps changing the Sun's direction of motion so that it moves in a circle.
parts.working: B1 gravity acts towards the centre of the galaxy; B1 this force changes the direction of motion (velocity) continuously.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'The galaxies are moving apart, so the galaxies themselves must be getting bigger.' Explain why this is incorrect.
parts.answer: The galaxies are not getting bigger; the space between the galaxies is expanding, so the galaxies move apart.
parts.working: B1 the space between galaxies expands (the galaxies themselves do not grow); B1 galaxies are held together by gravity so keep their size.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the expansion of the Universe suggests that, in the past, all the matter was much closer together.
parts.answer: If galaxies are moving apart now, they must have been closer together in the past. Going back in time, the Universe was smaller, hotter and denser.
parts.working: B1 galaxies were closer together in the past if they are moving apart now; B1 this leads to the idea of a very hot, dense start (the Big Bang).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what is meant by the Big Bang theory.
parts.answer: The theory that the Universe began from a very hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.
parts.working: B1 Universe began from a hot, dense state and has been expanding since.

practice.stem: The Sun is about 4.6 × 10⁹ years old. Its stable stage is expected to last about 1.0 × 10¹⁰ years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of its stable stage that the Sun has already completed. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many years the Sun has left in its stable stage.
parts.answer: 5.4 × 10⁹ years

parts.label: c
parts.text: A star with ten times the Sun's mass has a much shorter stable stage. Explain why.
parts.answer: Its stronger gravity compresses the core more, so it is hotter and fuses hydrogen much faster; it uses its fuel more quickly.
parts.working: B1 greater mass gives stronger gravity and a hotter core; B1 hydrogen is used up much faster, so the stable stage is shorter.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Approximately how long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
A 24 hours
B about one month
C about 365 days
D about 12 years
parts.answer: C about 365 days
parts.working: One orbit of the Sun takes about 365 days (one year). 24 hours is one rotation of the Earth on its axis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the main cause of the seasons on Earth?
A The distance between the Earth and the Sun changes a lot during the year.
B The Earth's axis is tilted relative to the plane of its orbit.
C The Moon blocks some sunlight during winter.
D The Sun gives out more energy in summer.
parts.answer: B The Earth's axis is tilted relative to the plane of its orbit.
parts.working: The tilted axis means each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for part of the year (higher Sun, longer days → summer). A is a common misconception: the Earth–Sun distance changes only slightly.

parts.label: a
