parts.text: Explain why there is day and night in Lahore.
parts.answer: The Earth rotates on its axis once in about 24 hours; Lahore faces the Sun for part of the rotation (day) and faces away for the rest (night).
parts.working: B1 Earth spins on its axis (every 24 h); B1 side facing the Sun has day, side facing away has night.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.
parts.answer: The Earth rotates from west to east, so the Sun appears to move across the sky in the opposite direction, from east to west.
parts.working: B1 Earth rotates west to east (anticlockwise seen from above the North Pole); B1 so Sun appears to move east to west.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In June the Sun is higher in the sky at midday in Lahore than in December. Explain why.
parts.answer: In June the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so the Sun's rays arrive more directly and the Sun is higher; in December it is tilted away.
parts.working: B1 tilt of the Earth's axis; B1 Northern Hemisphere tilted towards the Sun in June.

practice.stem: The start of the Islamic month is decided by sighting the thin crescent Moon after the new moon.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State approximately how long the Moon takes to orbit the Earth.
parts.answer: About one month (about 27 days).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Moon can be seen even though it does not give out its own light.
parts.answer: It reflects light from the Sun.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape (phases) during a month.
parts.answer: As the Moon orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half; at full moon we see all of the lit half, at new moon none of it.
parts.working: B1 half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun; B1 position in orbit changes how much of the lit half faces Earth.

practice.stem: A science club in Sialkot is making a display about the Solar System.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the star at the centre of the Solar System.
parts.answer: The Sun

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many planets there are in the Solar System and name the two closest to the Sun.
parts.answer: Eight planets; Mercury and Venus.
parts.working: B1 eight; B1 Mercury and Venus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Pluto was once called the ninth planet. State how it is now classified.
parts.answer: A dwarf planet (minor planet).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name two other types of object, apart from planets and dwarf planets, that orbit the Sun or a planet.
parts.answer: Any two of: asteroids; comets; natural satellites (moons).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is a natural satellite of the planet Mars?
A Titan
B Phobos
C Europa
D Io
parts.answer: B Phobos
parts.working: Phobos is one of the two small moons of Mars (the other is Deimos). Titan orbits Saturn, while Europa and Io orbit Jupiter.

practice.stem: The asteroid belt is a region of the Solar System containing many small rocky and metallic objects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where the asteroid belt is located in the Solar System.
parts.answer: Between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the two main materials from which asteroids are made.
parts.answer: Rock and metal.
parts.working: B1 rock and metal (for example iron and nickel).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a planet did not form from the material in the asteroid belt.
parts.answer: The strong gravity of Jupiter disturbed the orbits of the small objects so that they collided and broke apart, rather than joining together to form a planet.
parts.working: B1 Jupiter's gravity disturbs the objects' orbits; B1 they collide and break apart instead of joining.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a solar eclipse happens when the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth.
parts.answer: The Moon blocks the light from the Sun, casting a shadow on part of the Earth's surface.
parts.working: B1 the Moon blocks sunlight; B1 its shadow falls on the Earth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A solar eclipse does not happen at every new moon. Explain why.
parts.answer: The Moon's orbit is tilted by about 5° relative to the Earth's orbit around the Sun, so at most new moons the Moon passes above or below the Sun.
parts.working: B1 the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to the Earth's orbit (about 5°); B1 so at most new moons the Moon is not lined up with the Sun and Earth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the positions of the Sun, the Earth and the Moon during a lunar eclipse.
parts.answer: The Sun, Earth and Moon are in a straight line, with the Earth in the middle.
parts.working: B1 straight line with the Earth between the Sun and the Moon.

practice.stem: A student models the Earth's rotation. A ball on a stick (the Earth) is turned slowly on the spot while a lamp placed to one side shines on it. The lamp is kept still.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the lamp represents in this model.
parts.answer: The Sun.
parts.working: B1 the Sun gives the light that lights up one side of the Earth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student can show that the side facing the lamp is day and the side facing away is night.
parts.answer: Mark a spot on the ball. As the ball turns, the spot moves from the lit side into the dark side; the lit side is day and the dark side is night.
parts.working: B1 spot moves from the lit side to the dark side as the ball turns; B1 lit side = day, dark side = night.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the angle through which the ball turns in 6 hours, if one full turn of the ball represents 24 hours.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one limitation of this model.
parts.answer: It does not show the Earth's orbit around the Sun, or the tilt of the Earth's axis (or it is not to scale).
parts.working: B1 any one limitation (orbit not shown, tilt not shown, not to scale).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the Moon has no atmosphere.
parts.answer: Its gravity is too weak to hold on to gas molecules.
parts.working: B1 gravity too weak to hold gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe why the temperature of the Moon's surface changes greatly between day and night.
parts.answer: There is no atmosphere to retain thermal energy. In the day the surface gets very hot as it absorbs sunlight; at night it loses thermal energy to space and becomes very cold.
parts.working: B1 no atmosphere to trap or keep thermal energy; B1 very hot in the day (absorbs sunlight) and very cold at night (loses heat to space).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give one example of a natural satellite and one example of an artificial satellite.
parts.answer: Natural satellite: the Moon. Artificial satellite: for example a weather satellite or a GPS satellite.
parts.working: B1 Moon (or any natural moon); B1 any artificial satellite (weather, communication, GPS).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two uses of artificial satellites.
parts.answer: Any two of: communication (TV, telephone and internet signals), weather forecasting, navigation (GPS), observing the Earth or space.
parts.working: B1 for each of any two correct uses.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which planet is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the Solar System?
A Saturn
B Mars
C Jupiter
D Neptune
parts.answer: C Jupiter
parts.working: Order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Jupiter is fifth and the largest. Saturn is sixth.

practice.stem: The Earth moves around the Sun in an almost circular orbit of radius 1.5 × 10¹¹ m. One orbit takes 365 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the equation for the average orbital speed of an object in a circular orbit, defining each symbol.
parts.answer: v = 2πr ÷ T, where r is the orbital radius and T is the orbital period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average orbital speed of the Earth in m/s.
parts.answer: 2.99 × 10⁴ m/s (about 30 km/s)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the force that keeps the Earth in its orbit and the body that provides it.
parts.answer: Gravitational force (attraction) of the Sun.

practice.stem: The Moon orbits the Earth at an average distance of 3.84 × 10⁸ m with an orbital period of 27.3 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average orbital speed of the Moon. Give your answer in km/s to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student forgets to convert days to seconds. State the value of the speed she obtains and explain why it is not in m/s.
parts.answer: 8.84 × 10⁷ (metres per day) – it is a distance per day, not per second.
parts.working: B1 8.84 × 10⁷; B1 units are metres per day because T was in days.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the same side of the Moon always faces the Earth.
parts.answer: The Moon rotates on its axis once in the same time as it takes to orbit the Earth.

practice.stem:
Data for five planets:
planet: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter
distance from Sun / million km: 58, 108, 150, 228, 778
orbital period / Earth years: 0.24, 0.62, 1.00, 1.88, 11.9
mean surface temperature / °C: 167, 464, 15, −65, −110 (cloud tops)
mean density / g/cm³: 5.4, 5.2, 5.5, 3.9, 1.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between distance from the Sun and orbital period.
parts.answer: The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its orbital period (increasing more than proportionally).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the data to suggest why the inner four planets are rocky and Jupiter is a gas giant. Refer to how the Solar System formed.
parts.answer: The Solar System formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust by accretion; near the Sun it was too hot for light, volatile substances (hydrogen, helium, ices) to condense, so only rock and metal clumped together – high-density planets; further out it was cold enough for gases and ices to collect, so Jupiter is large with low density.
parts.working: B1 accretion of gas and dust (cloud/nebula); B1 high temperature near the Sun – only rocky/metal material condensed (high density); B1 colder further out – gases collected → low density gas giant.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Venus is further from the Sun than Mercury but is hotter. Explain why.
parts.answer: Venus has a thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide that traps infrared radiation (strong greenhouse effect); Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so it loses energy easily.
parts.working: B1 thick CO₂ atmosphere / greenhouse effect on Venus; B1 traps infrared emitted by the surface (Mercury has no atmosphere).

practice.stem: The average distance from the Sun to the Earth is 1.5 × 10¹¹ m and from the Sun to Jupiter is 7.78 × 10¹¹ m. The speed of light is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken for light to travel from the Sun to the Earth.
parts.answer: 500 s (about 8.3 minutes)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the time for light to travel from the Sun to Jupiter, in minutes.
parts.answer: 43 minutes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the strength of the Sun's gravitational field changes from the Earth's orbit to Jupiter's orbit, and state its effect on the orbital speed of the planets.
parts.answer: The field becomes weaker with increasing distance from the Sun, so planets further out have lower orbital speeds.
parts.working: B1 weaker further away; B1 lower orbital speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the Moon is correct?
A It produces its own light.
B It has a thick atmosphere of oxygen.
C Its gravitational field strength is less than that of the Earth.
D It is a planet that orbits the Sun.
parts.answer: C Its gravitational field strength is less than that of the Earth.
parts.working: The Moon has roughly one-eightieth of the Earth's mass and a smaller radius, so its gravitational field strength (about 1.6 N/kg) is much less than the Earth's 9.8 N/kg. A describes a star; B is wrong because the Moon has almost no atmosphere; D is wrong because the Moon orbits the Earth, not the Sun.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Distinguish between a meteoroid, a meteor and a meteorite.
parts.answer: Meteoroid: a small piece of rock or metal moving through space. Meteor: the streak of light seen when a meteoroid burns up in the Earth's atmosphere. Meteorite: a piece of rock that survives and lands on the Earth's surface.
parts.working: B1 meteoroid is in space; B1 meteor is the light streak in the atmosphere; B1 meteorite is the object that reaches the ground.

practice.stem: Venus orbits the Sun at an average distance of 1.08 × 10¹¹ m. Its orbital period is 224.7 Earth days. Treat its orbit as a circle and take 1 day = 86 400 s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the orbital period of Venus in seconds. Give your answer to 4 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average orbital speed of Venus in m/s. Use v = 2πr ÷ T. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Venus moves faster in its orbit than the Earth does, although both orbit the Sun. Explain why.
parts.answer: Venus is closer to the Sun, so the Sun's gravitational pull on it is stronger; this stronger pull provides the centripetal force for a smaller orbit that is traversed at a greater speed.
parts.working: B1 Venus is closer to the Sun, so the gravitational force (the centripetal force) is greater; B1 a greater speed is needed for a stable circular orbit at this smaller radius (v = √(GM/r) is larger for smaller r).

practice.stem: A geostationary satellite orbits the Earth at a radius of 4.2 × 10⁷ m from the centre of the Earth. Its orbital period is 24 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the orbital speed of the satellite in m/s. Use v = 2πr ÷ T. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the satellite appears to stay above the same point on the Earth's surface.
parts.answer: Its orbital period (24 hours) equals the period of the Earth's rotation, so it moves round at the same rate as the Earth turns. It orbits above the equator in the same direction as the Earth's rotation.
parts.working: B1 orbital period equals the Earth's rotation period (24 h); B1 so it stays over the same point (orbit above the equator).

practice.stem: A space probe travels at a constant speed of 1.2 × 10⁴ m/s over a distance of 7.8 × 10¹⁰ m.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time taken, in seconds, to travel this distance. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.working: M1 t = distance ÷ speed = 7.8 × 10¹⁰ ÷ 1.2 × 10⁴; A1 6.5 × 10⁶ s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert the time in part (a) into days. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 75 days

practice.stem: The Earth has a diameter of 1.27 × 10⁷ m and Mars has a diameter of 6.79 × 10⁶ m. Assume both planets are spheres.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio: volume of Mars ÷ volume of the Earth. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 ratio = (diameter of Mars ÷ diameter of Earth)³ = (6.79 ÷ 12.7)³; A1 0.15.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Mars has a mass of 0.107 times the mass of the Earth. Use your answer to part (a) to calculate the ratio of Mars' average density to the Earth's average density. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 density ratio = mass ratio ÷ volume ratio = 0.107 ÷ 0.153; A1 0.70 (so if the Earth's density is 5.5 g/cm³, Mars' is about 3.9 g/cm³).

practice.stem: A comet orbits the Sun in a very elongated (elliptical) orbit. At its closest it passes inside the orbit of Venus; at its furthest it is beyond Neptune.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where in its orbit the comet moves fastest.
parts.answer: Closest to the Sun.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain, in terms of energy, why the comet's speed changes around its orbit.
parts.answer: As the comet falls towards the Sun, gravitational potential energy is converted to kinetic energy, so it speeds up; as it moves away, kinetic energy is converted back to gravitational potential energy and it slows down; total energy is constant (conserved).
parts.working: B1 GPE → KE as it approaches the Sun; B1 KE → GPE moving away; B1 total energy conserved.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the gravitational force on the comet is greatest when it is nearest the Sun.
parts.answer: The gravitational force decreases with distance, so it is largest at the smallest distance.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the comet develops a bright tail only when it is close to the Sun.
parts.answer: Near the Sun it is heated, so ice turns to gas and releases dust, which reflects sunlight (and is pushed away from the Sun).

practice.stem: Io is a moon of Jupiter. It orbits at a radius of 4.22 × 10⁸ m with a period of 1.77 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average orbital speed of Io in m/s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Moon orbits the Earth at a similar radius of 3.84 × 10⁸ m with a speed of about 1.0 × 10³ m/s. Calculate how many times faster Io moves.
parts.answer: About 17 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Io moves much faster than the Moon even though their orbital radii are similar.
parts.answer: Jupiter has a much greater mass than the Earth, so its gravitational field (pull) at that distance is much stronger; a faster speed is needed to stay in orbit.
parts.working: B1 Jupiter much more massive; B1 stronger gravitational field/force at the same distance → greater orbital speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the Solar System formed according to the accretion model.
parts.answer: A large cloud of gas and dust (containing hydrogen, helium and heavier elements from earlier stars) began to collapse under gravity; it formed a rotating disc; most material collected at the centre to form the Sun; in the disc, dust and gas particles collided and stuck together (accretion), growing into planetesimals and then planets.
parts.working: B1 cloud of gas and dust collapses due to gravity; B1 rotating disc with Sun forming at the centre; B1 particles in the disc collide and clump together into planets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Sun contains more than 99 % of the mass of the Solar System.
parts.answer: Gravity pulled most of the cloud's material into the centre, where the Sun formed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why all the planets orbit the Sun in the same direction and in nearly the same plane.
parts.answer: They formed from the same rotating, flattened disc of material, so they kept its direction of rotation and its plane.
parts.working: B1 formed from a (flattened) disc; B1 the disc was rotating in one direction.

practice.stem: A robotic rover of mass 950 kg is sent to Mars.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the weight of the rover on Earth and on Mars. Gravitational field strength: Earth 9.8 N/kg; Mars 3.7 N/kg.
parts.answer: Earth: 9310 N; Mars: 3515 N
parts.working: C1 W = mg; A1 both values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the gravitational field strength at the surface of Mars is less than at the surface of the Earth.
parts.answer: Mars has a much smaller mass than the Earth (field strength at the surface depends on the planet's mass and radius).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Mars orbits the Sun at a radius of 2.28 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 687 Earth days. Calculate its orbital speed in km/s.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The Earth's orbital speed is about 30 km/s. Explain why Mars moves more slowly.
parts.answer: Mars is further from the Sun, where the Sun's gravitational field is weaker.

practice.stem: A spacecraft of mass 1200 kg orbits Mars in a circular orbit of radius 3.9 × 10⁶ m from the centre of Mars. It completes one orbit every 2.0 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the orbital speed of the spacecraft in m/s. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction of the resultant force on the spacecraft and name the force that provides it.
parts.answer: Towards the centre of Mars (the centre of its orbit); the force is the gravitational pull of Mars.
parts.working: B1 towards the centre of Mars; the gravitational pull of Mars provides the force.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The spacecraft's speed stays constant, but its velocity is changing. Explain why.
parts.answer: Velocity has both speed and direction. The direction of the spacecraft changes all the time as it moves around the circle, so its velocity changes.
parts.working: B1 velocity includes direction; B1 direction changes continuously in a circular orbit, so velocity changes although speed is constant.

practice.stem: Mercury is closer to the Sun than Venus. The day side of Mercury reaches about +430 °C and its night side falls to about −180 °C. The surface of Venus is about 460 °C everywhere.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Venus has a higher surface temperature than the day side of Mercury, even though Venus is further from the Sun.
parts.answer: Venus has a very thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide. Sunlight passes through and heats the surface, but the atmosphere traps the infrared radiation re-emitted by the surface, so the surface keeps getting hotter (greenhouse effect).
parts.working: B1 thick carbon dioxide atmosphere; B1 sunlight passes through to heat the surface; B1 atmosphere traps infrared radiation re-emitted from the surface (greenhouse effect).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the temperature of Mercury changes much more between its day side and its night side than the temperature on Venus does.
parts.answer: Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so it cannot keep thermal energy in at night and the night side becomes very cold. Venus's thick atmosphere keeps its temperature nearly the same everywhere.
parts.working: B1 Mercury has little or no atmosphere so heat is lost at night; B1 Venus's atmosphere retains and spreads thermal energy, keeping its temperature steady.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On 21 June the Sun is directly overhead at latitude 23.5° N. Lahore is at latitude 31.5° N. Calculate the angle of the Sun above the horizon at midday in Lahore on 21 June.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On 21 December the Sun is directly overhead at latitude 23.5° S. Calculate the angle of the Sun above the horizon at midday in Lahore on 21 December.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Sun's energy reaching each square metre of ground in Lahore is greater in June than in December.
parts.answer: In June the Sun is higher in the sky, so its rays strike the ground more directly and the same energy is spread over a smaller area. The days are also longer, so the Sun shines for more hours.
parts.working: B1 higher Sun means more direct rays and less spreading of energy (smaller area); B1 longer days give more hours of sunshine.

practice.stem: A student says: 'The seasons happen because the Earth is closer to the Sun in summer.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the student's idea is wrong. Use the fact that the Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
parts.answer: The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, which is winter in the Northern Hemisphere, so distance from the Sun is not the cause of the seasons.
parts.working: B1 closest to the Sun in early January (Northern winter), so distance is not the cause; B1 summer is caused by the tilt of the axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is summer in Australia in December.
parts.answer: In December the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so the Sun's rays strike the ground more directly and the days are longer.
parts.working: B1 southern hemisphere tilted towards Sun (more direct rays); B1 longer days give more energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the cause of the seasons.
parts.answer: The tilt of the Earth's axis (about 23.5°) relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
